p.seg: τὸ Δαῖραν κατ’ ἔλλειψίν ἐστι τοῦ ε διὰ τὸ μέτρον· Δάειραν γάρ ἐστι. λέγει δὲ τὴν Περσεφόνην, ὡς δηλοῖ [διά] τὸ μουνογένειαν. Νυχίαν δὲ εἶπεν ἤτοι διὰ τὸ χθονίων βασιλεύειν — νύκτα γὰρ τὸν ἀφώτιστον τόπον φασίν — ἢ ἣν νυκτὸς οὔσης ἱλάσκονται· εὔλογον γὰρ τὴν τῶν νυχίων τόπων κρατοῦσαν κατὰ τὴν τῆς νυκτὸς ὥραν ἱλάσκεσθαι. ὅτι δὲ Δαῖραν τὴν Περσεφόνην καλοῦσι, Τιμοσθένης ἐν τῷ Ἐξηγητικῷ (fg 12 Tresp Die Fragm. d. gr. Kultschr. 1914, 52) συγκατατίθεται, καὶ Αἰσχύλος ἐν Ψυχαγωγοῖς (fg 277 N.²) ἐμφαίνει, τὴν Περσεφόνην ἐκδεχόμενος Δαῖραν.

div.p: 846-47 a. Δαῖραν μουνογέ〈νειαν〉: Δαῖραν is an ellipsis of the ε for the sake of the meter; for it is Δάειραν. He means Persephone, as the word μουνογένειαν shows. He called her Νυχίαν either because she rules over the underworld—for they call the lightless place “night”—or because she is propitiated when it is night; for it is reasonable that the ruler of the nether regions is propitiated at the hour of night. That they call Persephone Δαῖρα, Timosthenes in his Exegeticus (fr. 12 Tresp, Die Fragm. d. gr. Kultschr. 1914, 52) agrees, and Aeschylus in the Psychagogi (fr. 277 N.²) indicates it, understanding Persephone as Δαῖρα.

div.p: 860. ἑπτὰ μὲν ἀενάοις: having bathed in the waters of seven ever-flowing rivers. He tells marvels.

p.seg: ἑπτάκις δέ, φησί, καὶ τὴν Ἑκάτην ἐπικαλέσασα· δοκοῦσι γὰρ αἱ φαρμακίδες τὴν Ἑκάτην ἐπάγεσθαι. Βριμὼ δὲ αὐτὴν προσηγόρευσε διὰ τὸ φοβερὸν καὶ καταπληκτικὸν τῆς δαίμονος καὶ φάσματα ἐπιπέμπειν τὰ καλούμενα Ἑκαταῖα καὶ πολλάκις αὑτῆς μεταβάλλειν τὸ εἶδος, διὸ καὶ Ἔμπουσαν καλεῖσθαι. ἢ παρὰ τὸν βρόμον τοῦ πυρός — ‘τόσσος γὰρ πέλεται βρόμος’ (Ξ 396) —, ἡ γὰρ θεὸς λαμπαδοῦχος. τὸ δὲ βρι ἐπιτάσεώς ἐστιν, ὡς τὸ ‘βριήπυος ὄβριμος Ἄρης’ (Ν 521)· ἴσως οὖν Βριμὼ ἡ μεγάλην ἔχουσα μῆνιν, βρίμηνίς τις οὖσα.

div.p: 861. ἑπτάκι δὲ Βριμώ: seven times, he says, she called upon Hecate; for sorceresses are thought to invoke Hecate. He called her Brimo because of the fearful and terrifying nature of the goddess and because she sends apparitions called Hecataea and often changes her own form, for which reason she is also called Empusa. Or from the roar of fire — 'for such is the roar' (Ξ 396) —, for the goddess is torch-bearing. The element βρι indicates intensity, as in 'βριήπυος ὄβριμος Ἄρης' (Ν 521); perhaps then Brimo is she who has great wrath, being a kind of βρίμηνις.

div.p:
Θησέως σωτηρίαν στέφανος αὐτῆς κατηστερίσθη. ὧν οὐδέτερον ἀληθές. καταλέλειπται γὰρ ὑπὸ Θησέως ἐν Νάξῳ· 〈δια〉πεπαρθένευται δὲ ὑπὸ Διονύσου κατά τινας, ἐξ ἧς παιδοποιεῖ Οἰνοπίωνα, Θόαντα, Στάφυλον, Λάτραμυν, Εὐάνθη, Ταυρόπολιν. ὅτι δὲ οὔτε Μίνως συνεχώρησεν τὸν γάμον Ἀριάδνης οὔτε ἤγαγεν αὐτὴν εἰς Ἀθήνας Θησεύς, Ὅμηρός φησι ῥητῶς, τελευτῆσαί 〈τε〉 αὐτὴν καταλειφθεῖσαν ὑπὸ Θησέως, δι’ ὧν ὁ Ὀδυσσεύς φησι (λ 321. 22. 24)·
‘Φαίδρην τε Πρόκριν τε ἴδον καλήν τ’ Ἀριάδνην,
κούρην Μίνωος ὀλοόφρονος, ἥν ποτε Θησεύς
γῆμεν οὐδ’ ἀπόνητο.’
ὅτι δὲ ὁ στέφανος ὑπὸ Διονύσου κατηστέρικται, Ἄρατός φησιν (Phaen. 71 sq.)·
‘αὐτοῦ κἀκεῖνος στέφανος, τὸν ἀγαυὸν ἔθηκεν
σῆμ’ ἔμεναι Διόνυσος ἀποιχομένης Ἀριάδνης.’

For Theseus' safety her crown was placed among the stars. Neither of these is true. For she was left behind by Theseus on Naxos; and she was deflowered by Dionysus according to some, from whom she bears Oenopion, Thoas, Staphylus, Latramys, Euanthes, Tauropolis. That Minos did not consent to the marriage of Ariadne nor did Theseus bring her to Athens, Homer says expressly, and that she died abandoned by Theseus, through what Odysseus says (λ 321. 22. 24): 'Phaedra and Procris I saw, and fair Ariadne, daughter of Minos of baneful mind, whom once Theseus married but had no joy of her.' That the crown was placed among the stars by Dionysus, Aratus says (Phaen. 71 sq.): 'there too is that crown, which glorious Dionysus set as a sign of departed Ariadne.'

p.seg:
τὸ Ὁμηρικὸν παρέφρασεν (Ψ 598 sq.)·
‘ἰάνθη δ’ ὡσεί τε περὶ σταχύεσσιν ἐέρση
ληίου ἀλδήσκοντος.’
τὸ μὲν οὖν τηκόμενον πάντως καὶ ἰαίνεται (μ 175 sq.)·
‘αἶψα δ’ ἰαίνετο κηρός, ἐπεὶ κέλετο μεγάλη ἴς
ἠελίοιο.’
οὐ πάντως δέ, εἴ τι ἰαίνεται, τοῦτο καὶ τήκεται. ὅθεν Ὅμηρος εἰπὼν ‘ἰάνθη’ ἐπήνεγκεν ‘ὡσεί τε’ μεταφορικῶς λέγων, ὥστε εἶναι τὸ νοούμενον ἐμφατικὸν τῆς τῶν σταχύων ἡδονῆς καθάπερ ἐμψύχων, τῆς δρόσου ἀντεχομένης τῶν καρπῶν, ὅτε ὀρθὸν ἔχουσι τὸν στάχυν οἷον μετεωριζόμενοι· οὕτω καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν τοῦ Μενελάου εἰς τέρψιν μετῆχθαι τοῖς λόγοις τοῦ Ἀντιλόχου. τὸ δὲ τήξει παραβάλλειν τὴν τερπομένην ψυχὴν οὐ πιθανόν.

div.p: 1019–21. τηκομένη οἷόν τε: he paraphrased the Homeric passage (Ψ 598 sq.): “and he warmed as when dew upon ears of a growing crop.” Now what melts certainly also warms (μ 175 sq.): “and quickly the wax warmed, since the great strength of the sun commanded it.” But not everything that warms also melts. Hence Homer, having said “warmed,” added “as when” speaking metaphorically, so that the meaning is expressive of the pleasure of the ears of grain as if they were alive, the dew clinging to the fruits when they hold their stalk upright, as if raised aloft; so too the soul of Menelaus was moved to delight by the words of Antilochus. But to compare the delighted soul to melting is not plausible.
δύναται οὖν ἀναγινώσκεσθαι καὶ τὸ τηκομένη ἐπὶ τέρψεως. τὸ γὰρ τηκόμενον πάντως, ὅτε λύεται, καὶ μαλάσσεται. ἔστιν οὖν εἰπεῖν, ὅτι πᾶσα διελύθη, ἐφηπλώθη ἡ Μήδεια.
It is possible, then, to read τηκομένη also in the sense of delight. For what melts, when it is loosened, certainly also becomes soft. So one can say that Medea was wholly dissolved, spread out.

div.p: b. ἔνθα Προμηθεύς· that Deucalion was the son of Prometheus and Pandora, Hesiod says in the first book of the Catalogues (fg 2 Rz.²), and that Hellen was the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, from whom the Hellenes and Hellas are named. That Deucalion ruled Thessaly, Hellanicus says in the first book of the Deucalioneia (4 fg 6 ab J.). That Deucalion also founded an altar of the twelve gods, Hellanicus says in the same work.

div.p: c. Iapetionides: From what woman Deucalion was born to Prometheus has been passed over in silence. There is also another Deucalion, about whom Hellanicus (4 fr. 114 J.) gives an account, and another, the son of Minos, about whom Pherecydes (3 fr. 85 J.), and a fourth, the son of Abas, whom Aristippus mentions in his Arcadica (fr. 3 M. IV 327).

div.p: οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ Θεσσαλοῦ τοῦ Φειδίππου πατρός, τοῦ Ἡρακλείδου, μετὰ τὰ Τρωικὰ κληθῆναί φασι. διαιρεῖται δὲ εἰς μέρη δ', Πελασγιώτιν, Θεσσαλιώτιν, Ἰωλκῖτιν, Φθιῶτιν. ταύτα παρατίθεται Ἀπολλόδωρος ἐν Νεῶν καταλόγῳ (244 fg 164 J.).

div.p: 1093. Of the Aeaean island: The syllable αι is redundant; for it is "of the Aean island," and Aea is the mother-city of the Colchians. He mentions the island in the Phasis, where the fleece was, as Pherecydes (3 fr. 100 J.) says.

p.seg: οὐκ ἀπὸ Αἰόλου, ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ τῶν Αἰόλου. Σισύφου γὰρ παῖδες ἐγένοντο ὁ Ἄλμος καὶ Πορφυρίων, Χρυσογόνης δὲ τῆς Ἄλμου καὶ Ποσειδῶνος Μινύας ὁ τὸν Ὀρχομενόν κτίσας. καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται Αἰολίδης, ὅτι Σίσυφος Αἰόλου ἐγένετο· Μινύας δὲ κατὰ μητέρα Αἰολίδης, πατρὸς δὲ Ποσειδῶνος. τοῦτον οὖν Ἀπολλώνιός φησιν εἰς τὴν Βοιωτίαν εἰσβαλόντα ὅμορον Θηβαίοις Ὀρχομενόν κτίσαι.

div.p: 1094-95. Aeolid Minyas: Not from Aeolus, but from the descendants of Aeolus. For the sons of Sisyphus were Almus and Porphyrion, and from Chrysogone, daughter of Almus, and Poseidon was born Minyas, who founded Orchomenus. And in this respect he is called Aeolid, because Sisyphus was the son of Aeolus; but Minyas is an Aeolid on his mother's side, and on his father's side a son of Poseidon. Apollonius, then, says that this man invaded Boeotia and founded Orchomenus on the border of Thebes.

Ἱππίας δὲ ὁ Ἠλεῖος ἐν Ἐθνῶν ὀνομασίαις (6 fg 1 J.) φησὶν ἔθνος τι καλεῖσθαι Σπαρτούς, καὶ ὁμοίως Ἀτρόμητος. Φερεκύδης δὲ ἐν τῇ ε' οὕτω φησίν (3 fg 22 a J.)· ‘ἐπεὶ δὲ Κάδμος κατῳκίσθη ἐν Θήβῃσιν, Ἄρης διδοῖ αὐτῷ καὶ Ἀθηναίῃ τοῦ ὄφιος τοὺς ἡμίσεις ὀδόντας, τοὺς δὲ ἡμίσεις Αἰήτῃ. καὶ ὁ Κάδμος αὐτίκα σπείρει αὐτοὺς εἰς τὴν ἄρουραν Ἄρεως κελεύσαντος, καὶ αὐτῷ ἀναφύονται πολλοὶ ἄνδρες ὡπλισμένοι. ὁ δὲ Κάδμος δείσας βάλλει αὐτοὺς λίθοισιν. οἱ δὲ δοκέοντες ὑφ’ ἑαυτῶν βάλλεσθαι, κρατέουσιν ἀλλήλους καὶ θνή-

div.p: b. Cadmus, when Europa: about Cadmus' arrival in Thebes, Lysimachus in his Collection of Theban Marvels (see scholion a) gives an account, and Hellanicus in the first book of his Phoronis (4 F 1a J.), relating that he also sowed the dragon's teeth at Ares' will, and five armed men were born: Udaeus, Chthonius, Pelorus, Hyperenor, Echion. But Apollonius thinks that many others also fought with one another. In the third book of the Titanography attributed to Musaeus (2 B 1 Diels-Kranz) it is said that Cadmus went from Delphi with the cow leading the way. Hippias of Elis in his Names of Peoples (6 F 1 J.) says that a certain people is called the Spartoi, and similarly Atrometus. Pherecydes in his fifth book says as follows (3 F 22a J.): 'When Cadmus settled in Thebes, Ares gave him and Athena half of the serpent's teeth, and the other half to Aeetes. And Cadmus immediately sows them in the field at Ares' command, and many armed men spring up for him. Cadmus, in fear, throws stones at them. They, thinking they are being pelted by each other, kill one another and die—'

div.p: e. Cadmus son of Agenor: he says that those left over in the battle settled in Thebes with Cadmus. Hellanicus also says (4 F 1b J.) that Cadmus took out the serpent's teeth and sowed them, and from them five men grew: Udaeus, Chthonius, Hyperenor, Echion, Pelorus. And Hellanicus says that only these sprang up, but Apollonius says that many others too—he established a crowd of earth-born men left over from Ares' reaping under the spear (v. 1186 f.)—and that they killed one another.

div.p: f. Some say Cadmus was the son of Agenor, others of Phoenix. Pherecydes in his fourth book says as follows (3 fg 21 J.): ‘Agenor, son of Poseidon, married Damno, daughter of Belus. Their children were Phoenix and Isaie, whom Aegyptus married, and Melia, whom Danaus married. Then Agenor married Argiope, daughter of the river Nile; their child was Cadmus.’

p.seg: λέγει τὴν ὑπὸ τὸν ὁρίζοντα δύσιν· 〈ἐρεμνὴν〉 γὰρ εἴρηκε 〈διὰ〉 τὸ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀρχαίων παραδεδομένον ἔρεβος. Αἰθίοπας δὲ λέγει τοὺς πρὸς τῇ δύσει, ἐρεμνὴν δὲ γῆν τὸ ἀφανὲς ἡμισφαίριον τὸ περὶ τὸ ἔρεβος· τοιοῦτο δὲ ἀκουστέον τὸν ὑπὸ τὸν ὁρίζοντα τόπον ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἀπολλωνίου. ἑσπέριον δὲ τὸν ἥλιον εἴρηκε, τὴν ὥραν σημαίνων, καθ' ἣν ὥραν παρέπεται αὐτῷ τὸ δύνειν. νεάτας δὲ ἄκριας εἴρηκεν τῶν Αἰθιόπων τὰς ἐσχατιὰς ὡς ὑπερκειμένας τῆς οἰκουμένης. οὐκ ὀρθῶς δὲ εἴρηκεν ὑπὲρ ἄκριας Αἰθιόπων τὸν ἥλιον δύνειν· ὁ γὰρ ὁρίζων κύκλος, οὐκ ὢν τῇ φύσει, τῇ ὄψει ἐπισημαίνεται.

div.p: 1191-92. The sun went down far away to the dark earth: he means the setting below the horizon; for he has said ‘dark’ because of the Erebus handed down by the ancients. He calls the Ethiopians those towards the setting, and ‘dark earth’ the invisible hemisphere around Erebus; such must be understood as the place below the horizon in Apollonius. He has called the sun ‘evening’, indicating the hour at which its setting follows. He has called the ‘uttermost peaks’ of the Ethiopians their farthest parts as lying beyond the inhabited world. But he has not correctly said that the sun sets beyond the peaks of the Ethiopians; for the horizon circle, not existing in nature, is marked by sight.

div.p: 1226. θώρηκα στάδιον: because it was not chain-mail, but a standing corselet; it is formed from 'standing'. But some say 'στάδιον' means well-made, which Callimachus also says (fg 59 Schn. = 145 Kapp): 'and he wore a well-made tunic'.

p.seg: Ἴσθμια τὰ ἐν Ἰσθμῷ τελούμενα τῆς Κορίνθου πρότερον μὲν τῷ Ποσειδῶνι, ὕστερον δὲ Μελικέρτῃ κατὰ κέλευσιν τοῦ τότε βασιλεύοντος Σισύφου τοῦ Αἰόλου· ὅτε προσβρασθὲν τὸ τοῦ Μελικέρτου σῶμα ἰδὼν τῇ Κορίνθῳ ἐπέγνω ἀδελφιδοῦν ὄντα καὶ Ἀθάμαντος τοῦ Αἰόλου υἱόν, ἐτίμησεν, ὡς ἔδει, καὶ τῷ ἀγῶνι τῷ Ἰσθμικῷ, ἐν ᾧ οἱ νικῶντες πίτυϊ ἐστέφοντο πάλαι, ὕστερον δὲ ξηρῷ σελίνῳ. Μουσαῖος δὲ ἐν τῷ Περὶ Ἰσθμίων (M. IV 518) δύο φησὶ γίνεσθαι ἀγῶνας ἐν Ἰσθμῷ, καὶ τὸν μὲν Ποσειδῶνος εἶναι, τὸν δὲ Μελικέρτου.

div.p: 1240. οἷος δ’ Ἴσθμιον: The Isthmian games are those celebrated at the Isthmus of Corinth, formerly in honor of Poseidon, but later in honor of Melicertes at the command of the then king Sisyphus son of Aeolus; when he saw the body of Melicertes washed ashore at Corinth, he recognized that it was his nephew, the son of Athamas son of Aeolus, and honored him, as was fitting, also with the Isthmian contest, in which the victors were crowned with pine in old times, but later with dry celery. But Musaeus in his work On the Isthmian Games (M. IV 518) says that two contests take place at the Isthmus, one of Poseidon and one of Melicertes.

div.p: 1241. ἢ Ταίναρον: Taenarum is a promontory of Laconia. Lerna is a spring of Argos sacred to Poseidon: 'surpassing hierophant of the Lernaian sanctuaries' (Anth. Pal. IX 688, 4).
div.note: 20 Et. Gen. (AB) Ταίναρος: III 1240—1242. Ἴσθμιον(!) τόπος ἐν Κορίνθῳ, ἰσθμὸς δὲ στενὴ θάλασσα (immo v. sch. I 936/49 g). Ταίναρον δὲ 〈..., Λέρνη δὲ add. W〉 κρήνη ἐν Ἄργει· Ὑαντίου δὲ τοῦ Βοιωτικοῦ ἄλσους(!) ἀπὸ Ὕαντος οἰκίσαντος (Miller, -ήσαντος AB). Ὀγχηστὸς δὲ (δὲ B, om. A) πόλις τῆς (τῆς A, om. B) Βοιωτίας.

20 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) Ταίναρος: III 1240–1242. Ἴσθμιον(!) a place in Corinth, but an isthmus is a narrow sea (rather see scholion on I 936/49 g). Ταίναρον is 〈..., Λέρνη added by W〉 a spring in Argos; and of Hyantius the Boeotian grove(!) from Hyas having founded it (Miller, -ήσαντος in AB). Ὀγχηστὸς is (δὲ in B, omitted in A) a city of (τῆς in A, omitted in B) Boeotia.

div.p: 1242–43a. Of Hyantian Onchestus: of Boeotian; for the Hyantes formerly inhabited Boeotia. Onchestus is a city of Boeotia sacred to Poseidon. Homer (Iliad 2.506): 'and sacred Onchestus, the splendid grove of Poseidon.'

div.p: b. Hyantian instead of Boeotian; for the Hyantes are a barbarian people of Boeotia, whence also the proverb 'Boeotian pig.' And Calaureia is also sacred to Poseidon, as Philostephanus says (fr. 18 M. III 31); but formerly it belonged to Apollo, and Pytho to Poseidon, and they exchanged [that is, they swapped].

ἀντὶ τοῦ κέντρῳ. ἄκαινα δέ ἐστι μέτρον δεκάπουν, Θεσσαλῶν εὕρεμα, ἢ ῥάβδος ποιμενικὴ παρὰ Πελασγοῖς ηὑρημένη· περὶ ἧς Καλλίμαχός φησιν (fg 214 Schn. = 7, 7 Pfeiffer)·
‘ἀμφότερον, κέντρον τε βοῶν καὶ μέτρον ἀρούρης.’

div.p: b. ἀκαίνῃ: instead of κέντρῳ. ἄκαινα is a measure of ten feet, an invention of the Thessalians, or a shepherd's staff discovered among the Pelasgians; concerning which Callimachus says (fg 214 Schn. = 7, 7 Pfeiffer): 'both, a goad for oxen and a measure of the field.'
div.note: 5 Et. Gen. (B Voss.) ἄκαινα: ἡ ῥάβδος. Ἀπολλώνιος III 1323. Θεσσαλική ἐστι ῥάβδος, τὸ καλούμενον βούκεντρον. ὠνομάσθη δὲ οὕτως. Νεῖλος ὁ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ποταμός, ἀναβλύζων καὶ ἀνερχόμενος διὰ τοῦ θέρους, τὰ ὅρια τῆς γῆς τῶν Αἰγυπτίων τῇ ὑγρασίᾳ λύων καὶ μιγνὺς ἀπώλλυεν (Et. M., ἀπώλυμεν B, ἀπόλλομεν Voss.). ἐλαττουμένου (Voss., ἐλαττομ- B) δὲ αὐτοῦ καὶ πάλιν (B, πάλιν καὶ Voss.) καταβαίνοντος μάχη καὶ ἀμφισβήτησις τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις (B, τῶν -ων Voss.) περὶ ὁρίων τοσαύτη ἐγίνετο, ὥστε καὶ ἀλλήλους φονεύειν. ὕστερον δὲ ῥάβδον λαβόντες τὰς ἑαυτῶν γαίας ἐγεωμέτρουν πρὸ (Voss., περὶ B) τῆς ἀναβάσεως τοῦ ποταμοῦ καὶ ἐσημειοῦντο, καὶ πάλιν μετὰ τὴν ἀπόβασιν τοῦ ποταμοῦ τῇ αὐτῇ ῥάβδῳ γεωμετροῦντες, ἕκαστος τὴν ἰδίαν γῆν ἀπελάμβανε δίχα μάχης καὶ φόνου. ἐκλήθη οὖν ἡ ῥάβδος ἐκείνη ἄκαινα, δι’ ἧς ἐγεωμέτρουν, ἡ στεροῦσα αὐτοὺς τοῦ καίνειν ἀλλήλους, ὅ ἐστι φονεύειν. λέγεται δέ, ὅτι Θεσσαλός τις εὑρεθεὶς ἐν τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ ἐπενοήσατο τῇ ῥάβδῳ γεωμετρεῖν τὴν γῆν. ἔνθεν καὶ Πελασγίδι εἶπεν ἀντὶ τοῦ Θεσσαλικῇ. ἐργατίνης δὲ ὁ γεωργός (ἐργ. δὲ ὁ γ. hic in Et. M., ὁ γ. post Ἀπολλώνιος in B, om. Voss.). cf. W 80 Hesych. ἄκαινα Συν. ἀ. (46, 5 Ba. Phot. Suid.) Eust. 911, 51

5 Etymologicum Genuinum (B, Voss.) ἄκαινα: the rod. Apollonius III 1323. It is a Thessalian rod, the so-called ox-goad. It was named thus: The Nile, the river of the Egyptians, rising and swelling during the summer, loosening the boundaries of the land of the Egyptians with its moisture and mixing them up, destroyed them (Et. M., ἀπώλυμεν in B, ἀπόλλομεν in Voss.). But when it diminished and again (B, πάλιν καὶ in Voss.) subsided, such fighting and dispute arose among the Egyptians (B, τῶν -ων in Voss.) over boundaries that they even killed one another. Later, taking a rod, they measured their own lands before (Voss., περὶ in B) the rising of the river and marked them, and again after the subsiding of the river, measuring with the same rod, each received his own land without fighting and slaughter. Therefore that rod, by which they measured, was called ἄκαινα, which deprived them of killing one another, that is, murdering. It is said that a certain Thessalian, being in Egypt, devised measuring the land with the rod. Hence he also said 'Pelasgian' instead of 'Thessalian'. And ἐργατίνης is the farmer (ἐργ. δὲ ὁ γ. here in Et. M., ὁ γ. after Ἀπολλώνιος in B, omitted in Voss.). cf. W 80 Hesych. ἄκαινα Συν. ἀ. (46, 5 Ba. Phot. Suid.) Eust. 911, 51
16 1342. Et. Gen. (B) ἐργατίναι: οἱ γηπόνοι. οἷον III 1340—1342.

div.p: 1377-79. οἷος δ’ οὐρανόθεν πυρόεις ἀναπάλλεται: it is also written ἀπολάμπεται. He speaks about the stars that dart across and quickly disappear, which by the swiftness of their motion have something similar to one rushing upon [something]. He calls ὁλκός the light that is dragged along with it by its swiftness. Such appearances Musaeus (2 B 17 Diels-Kranz) says rise from the ocean and are extinguished in the aether. Apollonius plausibly called the stars mentioned by Musaeus 'flashes'; for the gleams that occur, imperceptible because of their swiftness, are called 'flashes' from some source. But it is implausible to compare Jason, as he goes to a dangerous contest, to such a star, which is extinguished immediately upon appearing. But if someone should say that he has likened him to Pyroeis, about whom Epigenes in his work On the Chaldean Mathematics, after first speaking about the planets, of which he says one is Pyroeis, called by the Greeks Ares, but by the Chaldeans Heracles 〈...〉; for he says that as it moves along, flashes and sparks occur, but Pyroeis is slow-moving.

div.p: Μουσαῖος (2 B 17 Diels-Kranz) ἀναφερομένας φησὶν ἐκ τοῦ ὠκεανοῦ κατὰ τὸν αἰθέρα ἀποσβέννυσθαι. τοὺς δὲ ὑπὸ Μουσαίου ἀστέρας εἰρημένους Ἀπολλώνιος πιθανῶς μαρμαρυγὰς εἴρηκε· τὰς γὰρ γινομένας ἀκαταλήπτους διὰ τὴν ὀξύτητα ἀποστίλψεις ἀφ’ οὗτινος μαρμαρυγὰς καλοῦσιν. ἀπίθανον δὲ τῷ τοιούτῳ ἀστέρι παραβαλεῖν τὸν Ἰάσονα πρὸς ἐπικίνδυνον ἆθλον πορευόμενον, τῷ ἅμα τῷ φανῆναι εὐθέως σβεννυμένῳ. εἰ δέ τις λέγοι τῷ Πυρόεντι αὐτὸν ὡμοιωκέναι, περὶ οὗ Ἐπιγένης ἐν τῷ Περὶ τῶν Χαλδαϊκῶν μαθηματικῶν προειπὼν περὶ τῶν πλανητῶν, [λέγων] ὧν φησιν ἕνα εἶναι τὸν Πυρόεντα, προσαγορευόμενον [δὲ] ὑπὸ μὲν Ἑλλήνων Ἄρεως, ὑπὸ δὲ Χαλδαίων Ἡρακλέους 〈...〉· φησὶ γὰρ καὶ ἐπισυρομένου αὐτοῦ μαρμαρυγὰς καὶ σπινθῆρας γίνεσθαι, ὁ δὲ Πυρόεις δυσκίνητός ἐστιν.

Musaeus (2 B 17 Diels-Kranz) says that the appearances rise from the ocean and are extinguished in the aether. Apollonius plausibly called the stars mentioned by Musaeus 'flashes'; for the gleams that occur, imperceptible because of their swiftness, are called 'flashes' from some source. But it is implausible to compare Jason, as he goes to a dangerous contest, to such a star, which is extinguished immediately upon appearing. But if someone should say that he has likened him to Pyroeis, about whom Epigenes in his work On the Chaldean Mathematics, after first speaking about the planets, of which he says one is Pyroeis, called by the Greeks Ares, but by the Chaldeans Heracles 〈...〉; for he says that as it moves along, flashes and sparks occur, but Pyroeis is slow-moving.

div.head: Περιοχὴ τοῦ δ' τῶν Ἀργοναυτικῶν
div.p: Τοῦ δ' τῶν Ἀργοναυτικῶν τὰ κεφάλαιά ἐστι ταῦτα.

οἱ Ἀργοναῦται διαπεράσαντες τὸν Πόντον ὡς ἐπὶ τὸν Ἴστρον, διὰ τοῦ ποταμοῦ κατηνέχθησαν καὶ ἐπεραιώθησαν εἰς τὸ πάλαι μὲν καλούμενον Κρόνιον 〈πέλαγος, νῦν δὲ Ἀδρίαν〉· ἔνθα καὶ ἀναιροῦσι τὸν Ἄψυρτον δόλῳ. ἀγανακτοῦντος δὲ τοῦ Διὸς ἐπὶ τούτῳ καὶ δυσπνοίᾳ θέλοντος παρατρέψαι τοὺς Ἀργοναύτας, Ἥρα ἐπιπέμπει ἀνέμους, καὶ διὰ τοῦ Ἠριδανοῦ εἰς τὴν περὶ Σαρδὼ καταφέρονται θάλασσαν, καθαίρονται δὲ ὑπὸ Κίρκης· καὶ διαπλέουσι τὰς Πλαγκτὰς πέτρας, Θέτιδος μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων Νηρεΐδων προπεμπούσης, τὰς δὲ Σειρῆνας παραπλέουσι. διασωθέντες δὲ εἰς τὴν πάλαι μὲν Δρεπάνην, αὖθις δὲ κληθεῖσαν Κέρκυραν, τοὺς διὰ τῶν Συμπληγάδων διώκοντας αὐτοὺς Κόλχους καταλαμβάνουσιν, οἵτινες τὸν Ἀλκίνουν ἐξῃτοῦντο τὴν Μήδειαν. ὁ δὲ ὑπερθέμενος εἰς τὴν αὔριον, ἔφη παρθένον μὲν οὖσαν τῷ πατρὶ ἀποστέλλεσθαι, εἰ δὲ γυνὴ εἴη, παραδίδοσθαι τῷ ἀνδρί. γίνεται οὖν ὁ γάμος ἐκείνῃ τῇ νυκτί, καὶ οὕτως ἄπρακτοι γενόμενοι οἱ Κόλχοι μένουσιν ἐν τῇ Σχερίᾳ, δεδοικότες ἐπανελθεῖν πρὸς Αἰήτην. ἀποπλεύσαντες δὲ οἱ Ἀργοναῦται κατασύρονται τῆς Λιβύης εἰς Σύρτιν. καὶ τελευτῶσι μὲν Κάνθος καὶ Μόψος, ἀποροῦσι δὲ περὶ σωτηρίας τοῖς Ἀργοναύταις ἐπιφαίνεται Τρίτων καὶ ὡς διασωθήσονται δηλοῖ. βαστάσαντες οὖν τὴν ναῦν ἐκόμισαν εἰς τὴν Τριτωνίδα λίμνην. εἶτα γίνονται ἐν Κρήτῃ, ᾗ εἴργοντο προσελθεῖν ὑπὸ Τάλω· ὃν ἐπῳδαῖς ἠφάνισε Μήδεια. μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα παραγίνονται εἰς Αἴγιναν κἀκεῖθεν διασῴζονται εἰς Θεσσαλίαν.

p.seg: ἐλλείπει τὸ ὦ μόριον, ἵνα ᾖ ὦ θεά. ὁ δὲ νοῦς· αὐτὴ νῦν ἐμοὶ εἰπέ, ὦ Μοῦσα, τόν τε μόχθον καὶ τὰς βουλὰς Μηδείας, ἀποροῦντός μου, ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι εἰπεῖν, πότερον ἐρωτικῷ πάθει ἢ κακώσεως φυγὴν ποιουμένη κατέλιπε τὴν πατρίδα.

div.p: 1-5a. Now, goddess, the toil: the particle “O” is omitted, so that it would be “O goddess.” The sense: now tell me yourself, O Muse, both the toil and the counsels of Medea, since I am at a loss, so as not to be able to say whether it was through erotic passion or by making an escape from ill-treatment that she left her fatherland.

p.seg: ἤτοι κατὰ πρόσθεσιν τοῦ ε· ἔστι γὰρ ἀλγεινότατον, παρὰ τὸ ἀλγεῖν εἰρημένον. ἢ εἴρηται τὸ τὰς φροντίδας ἔχον, ὥστε τὴν λέξιν εἶναι παρὰ τὸ ἀλέγειν.

div.p: 11. Most painful: either by addition of the ε; for it is “most painful,” derived from “to suffer pain.” Or it is said to mean “having cares,” so that the word is from “to care for.”

p.seg: κεμάς ἐστιν ἡ νέα ἔλαφος. διαφορὰν δέ φασιν εἶναι κεμάδος καὶ νεβροῦ· κεμάδα γὰρ εἶναι τὴν ἔτι κοιμωμένην ἐν τῷ σπηλαίῳ, οἷον κοιμάδα τινὰ οὖσαν, νεβρὸν δὲ τὸν ἤδη μείζονα καὶ ἐπὶ βοράν ἐξιόντα καὶ νεμόμενον.

div.p: 12. And she trembled like some: a κεμάς is a young deer. They say there is a difference between a κεμάς and a fawn: for a κεμάς is one still sleeping in the cave, being as it were a “sleeper” (κοιμάς), while a fawn is one already larger and going out to pasture and feeding.

p.seg: ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴω γέγονε ῥήματος κατὰ διαίρεσιν ὀίω 〈...〉. μήποτε δὲ καί τὸ ‘δοάσσατο’ (Hom.) περισσῷ κέχρηται τῷ δ, ὡς καὶ τὸ ‘δνοφερὸν ὕδωρ’ (Hom.)· παρὰ γὰρ τὸ νέφος πεποίηται. καὶ παρὰ τὸ ἷψαι Σοφοκλῆς ἐν Ἰξίονι (fg 296 Pearson) δίψιόν φησι

div.p: 14. He thought: from the verb “οἴω” comes “ὀίω” by diaeresis 〈...〉. Perhaps also “δοάσσατο” (Homer) uses the δ redundantly, as also “δνοφερὸν ὕδωρ” (Homer); for it is formed from “νέφος.” And from “ἷψαι” Sophocles in Ixion (fr. 296 Pearson) says “δίψιον”

div.p: 46. πέζαν: the edge of the tunic, which we call ᾤα; for formerly a sheepskin was sewn on to prevent it from being worn away.

p.seg: χαλεπὰς καὶ κακάς. ἢ τὰς ἐπὶ κακῷ ἀναδιδομένας ἐκ τῆς γῆς· πλείονα γὰρ τῶν σωτηρίων τὰ φθοροποιά. ἢ τὰς δυσχερῶς σινομένας.

div.p: 52. ἀμφί τε δυσπαλέας: difficult and evil. Or those that spring up from the earth for harm; for the destructive are more numerous than the wholesome. Or those that are hard to injure.
div.note: 18 Et. Gen. (AB) δυσπαλέας ῥίζας: IV 52. τὰς κακῶς ἀναδιδομένας, ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλω. ἢ δυσχερῶς γινομένας (v. supra). Ἀπολλώνιος (Ἀπ. A, om. B).
18 Et. Gen. (AB) δυσπαλέας ῥίζας: IV 52. those that spring up badly, from πάλλω. Or those that come into being with difficulty (see above). Apollonius (Ἀπ. in A, omitted in B).

p.seg:
Ἥλιος καὶ Σελήνη Ὑπερίονος τοῦ Τιτᾶνος καὶ Θείας εἰσὶ παῖδες, ὡς Ἡσίοδός φησι (Theog. 371)·
‘Θεία δ’ Ἠέλιον τέκε λαμπράν τε Σελήνην.’

div.p: 54. τὴν δὲ νέον Τιτηνίς: Helios and Selene are children of Hyperion the Titan and Theia, as Hesiod says (Theog. 371): 'Theia bore Helios and bright Selene.'

p.seg: 57—58. οὐκ ἄρ’ ἐγὼ μούνη μετὰ Λάτμιον:

Λάτμος ὄρος Καρίας, ἔνθα ἔστιν ἄντρον, ἐν ᾧ διέτριβεν Ἐνδυμίων. ἔστι δὲ καὶ πόλις ἡ λεχθεῖσα Ἡράκλεια. λέγεται δὲ κατέρχεσθαι εἰς τοῦτο τὸ ἄντρον τὴν Σελήνην πρὸς Ἐνδυμίωνα. περὶ δὲ τοῦ τῆς Σελήνης ἔρωτος ἱστοροῦσι Σαπφὼ (fg inc. lib. 83 Lobel = 134 B. III 132) καὶ Νίκανδρος ἐν β' Εὐρωπείας (fg 24 Schn.).

div.p: 57-58. οὐκ ἄρ’ ἐγὼ μούνη μετὰ Λάτμιον: Latmus is a mountain of Caria, where there is a cave in which Endymion used to dwell. There is also a city called Heracleia. Selene is said to descend into this cave to Endymion. About the love of Selene Sappho (fg inc. lib. 83 Lobel = 134 B. III 132) and Nicander in the second book of the Europeia (fg 24 Schn.) tell the story.

τὸν δὲ Ἐνδυμίωνα Ἡσίοδος (fg 11 Rz.²) μὲν Ἀεθλίου τοῦ Διὸς καὶ Καλύκης, παρὰ Διὸς εἰληφότα τὸ δῶρον ἵν’ αὐτῷ ταμίαν εἶναι θανάτου, ὅτε θέλοι ὀλέσθαι 〈...〉 καὶ Πείσανδρος (16 fg 7 J.) καὶ Ἀκουσίλαος (2 fg 36 J.) καὶ Φερεκύδης (3 fg 121 J.) καὶ Νίκανδρος ἐν β' Αἰτωλικῶν (fg 6 Schn.) καὶ Θεόπομπος ὁ ἐποποιός. φασὶ δὲ αὐτὸν οἱ μὲν †Σπαρτιάτην†, οἱ δὲ Ἠλεῖον· Ἴβυκος δὲ ἐν α' (fg 44 B. III 249) Ἤλιδος αὐτὸν βασιλεῦσαί φησι.

Hesiod (fg 11 Rz.²) says that Endymion was the son of Aethlius, son of Zeus, and Calyce, and that he received from Zeus the gift to be the steward of his own death, whenever he wished to perish 〈...〉; and Peisander (16 fg 7 J.) and Acusilaus (2 fg 36 J.) and Pherecydes (3 fg 121 J.) and Nicander in the second book of the Aetolica (fg 6 Schn.) and Theopompus the epic poet. They say that he was †Spartiate†, but others say Elean; Ibycus in the first book (fg 44 B. III 249) says that he was king of Elis.
ἐν δὲ ταῖς Μεγάλαις Ἠοίαις (Hes. fg 148 Rz.²) λέγεται τὸν Ἐνδυμίωνα ἀνενεχθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ Διὸς εἰς οὐρανόν, ἐρασθέντα δὲ Ἥρας· εἰδώλῳ παραλογισθῆναι [τὸν ἔρωτα] νεφέλης καὶ ἐκβληθέντα κατελθεῖν

In the Great Ehoiai (Hes. fr. 148 Rz.²) it is said that Endymion was carried up to heaven by Zeus, and that he fell in love with Hera; he was deceived by a phantom of a cloud, and after being cast out he came down.

div.p: εἰς Ἅιδου. Ἐπιμενίδης (3 B 14 Diels-Kranz) δὲ αὐτὸν παρὰ θεοῖς διατρίβοντα ἐρασθῆναί φησι τῆς Ἥρας, διόπερ Διὸς χαλεπήναντος αἰτήσασθαι διὰ παντὸς καθεύδειν. τινὲς δὲ διὰ 〈τὴν〉 πολλὴν δικαιοσύνην ἀποθεωθῆναί φασιν αὐτὸν καὶ 〈...〉 αἰτήσασθαι παρὰ Διὸς ἀεὶ καθεύδειν.

To Hades. Epimenides (3 B 14 Diels-Kranz) says that he, while spending time among the gods, fell in love with Hera, and that therefore, when Zeus became angry, he asked to sleep forever. Some say that because of his great righteousness he was deified and asked from Zeus to sleep always.

ἔνιοι δὲ ἀναιροῦσι τὸν ἐπὶ τῷ Ἐνδυμίωνος ὕπνῳ μῦθον. φιλοκύνηγον γὰρ αὐτὸν γενόμενον, νύκτωρ πρὸς τῇ σελήνῃ κυνηγεῖν διὰ τὸ ἐξιέναι τὰ θηρία κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν καιρὸν ἐπὶ τὰς νομάς, τὰς δὲ ἡμέρας ἐν σπηλαίῳ αὐτὸν ἀναπαύεσθαι, ὥς τινας οἴεσθαι πάντοτε αὐτὸν κοιμᾶσθαι. οἱ δὲ ἀλληγοροῦσι τὸν μῦθον, λέγοντες ὡς ἄρα Ἐνδυμίων πρῶτος ἐπεχείρησε τῇ περὶ τὰ μετέωρα φιλοσοφίᾳ, παρασχεῖν δὲ αὐτῷ τὰς ἀφορμὰς τὴν σελήνην ἔν τε φωτισμοῖς καὶ κινήσεσιν, δι’ ὃ καὶ νύκτωρ σχολάζοντα τούτοις ὕπνῳ μὴ χρῆσθαι, κοιμᾶσθαι δὲ μεθ’ ἡμέραν. τινὲς δὲ τῷ ὄντι φίλυπνόν τινα γεγονέναι τὸν Ἐνδυμίωνα, ἀφ’ οὗ καὶ παροιμία ‘Ἐνδυμίωνος ὕπνος’ ἐπὶ τῶν πολὺ κοιμωμένων ἢ ἀμελῶς τι πραττόντων ὡς δοκεῖν κοιμᾶσθαι.

Some reject the myth about Endymion's sleep. For they say that he was fond of hunting, and at night he hunted by the light of the moon because the wild beasts come out at that time to their pastures, and during the days he rested in a cave, so that some thought he was always sleeping. Others allegorize the myth, saying that Endymion was the first to attempt philosophy concerning the heavens, and that the moon provided him with starting points in its illuminations and movements, for which reason he spent his nights on these studies and did not sleep, but slept during the day. Some say that Endymion was in fact a lover of sleep, from which comes the proverb 'Endymion's sleep' applied to those who sleep a lot or do something carelessly so as to seem to be asleep.
καὶ Θεόκριτος μέμνηται (III 49 sq.)·
And Theocritus mentions it (III 49 sq.):

div.p: 59-61a. Truly often indeed you too: it is told that sorceresses draw down the moon with their spells. The Thessalian women are thought to do this, having failed in their assumption; according to which Aglaonice, daughter of Hegemon, being experienced in astronomy and knowing the eclipses of the moon, whenever they were about to occur, claimed to draw down the goddess,
div.note: 20 τοῦτο λέγει, ἐπειδὴ μυθεύονται, ὡς ἄρα αἱ φαρμακίδες τὴν σελήνην κατασπῶσι ταῖς ἐπῳδαῖς. καὶ μάλιστα δοκοῦσι τοῦτο ποιεῖν αἱ Θετταλαί, ὡς καὶ Ἀριστοφάνης (Nub. 749 sq.)· ‘γυναῖκα φαρμακίδα πριάμενος Θετταλὴν νύκτωρ τὴν σελήνην καθέλοιμι δι’ αὐτῆς’ ceteris praetermissis A. cf. W 30

20 This he says, since it is told that sorceresses draw down the moon with their spells. div.p: b. Remembering love: that of Endymion through your spells. And dark in the moonless night, because of my occupation with the beloved. Some interpret the eclipse of the moon as being caused by sorceresses drawing it down, and the ancients called eclipses 'drawings down'.

γέγονε μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ πέρας καὶ περαία καὶ τὸ περαιόθεν. ὅθεν καὶ ἤπειρος λέγεται πᾶσα ἡ γῆ καταχρηστικῶς, κυρίως δὲ ἡ εἰς ἄπειρον ἐκβάλλουσα, ὡς φανερὸν Εὐριπίδης πεποίηκεν (fg 1010 N.²)·

div.p: 71. περαιόθεν: it is formed from πέρας and περαία and περαιόθεν. Hence all land is called ἤπειρος by catachresis, but properly it is that which extends to infinity, as Euripides has made clear (fr. 1010 N.²): ‘ἤπειρον εἰς ἄπειρον ἐκβάλλων χθόνα.’

div.p: 87. δώσω δὲ χρύσειον: Apollonius has Medea, after fleeing from Aeetes' house, promising the fleece to Jason; but the author of the Naupactica (fr. 9 Kink.) has her carrying out the fleece with her during her flight, it being kept in his own house [of Aeetes]; but Herodorus (31 fr. 52 J.) says that after the yoking of the wild bulls Jason was sent by Aeetes for the fleece, and that he went and killed the dragon and brought the fleece to Aeetes, and that he treacherously invited them to dinner.

Μητρόδωρος δὲ ἐν α' τῶν Περὶ Τιγράνην (184 fg 1 J.) τὸν Θερμώδοντα Ἀράξην φησὶ λέγεσθαι. Καυκασίαν δὲ θάλασσαν τὴν Κασπίαν φησὶ διὰ τὸ συνάπτειν τῷ Καυκάσῳ.

div.p: b. far from Titanian Aea: of the Titan river, from which the land is also called Titanis; Eratosthenes mentions it in his Geography (fg III B 76 Berger). The Lycus river, flowing from the Araxes, mingles with the Phasis, and thus losing its own name it flows into the sea. The same thing happens with the Onochonus in Thessaly and the Peneius and the Pamisus; for when they flow together, they are called Peneius. The Araxes is a river of Scythia. Metrodorus in the first book of his On Tigranes (184 fg 1 J.) says that the Thermodon is called Araxes. He says the Caucasian sea is the Caspian because it borders the Caucasus.

p.seg: πολλάς. ὑπερβολικῶς καὶ τοῦτο εἴρηκε διαγράφων τὸ τέρας τοῦ δράκοντος. ῥυμβόνας δὲ τὰς εἱλήσεις τῆς σπείρας, τὰς περιδινήσεις. — καὶ Εὐριπίδης ἐν Πειρίθῳ (fg 593 N.²): ‘σὲ τὸν αὐτοφυῆ πάντων [θεῶν] αἰθέρα ῥύμβῳ’, τουτέστιν ἐν κινήσει, ὅθεν καὶ τὸ κινούμενον τροχίσκιον ὑπὸ τῶν φαρμακίδων ῥυμβίον καλεῖται. καὶ παρ’ Εὐπόλιδι (fg 72 Kock I 274)· ‘ὦ ῥύμβε, μαστίξας ἐμέ’, οὕτω δὲ λέγουσι τὰς περιφερεῖς κινήσεις.

div.p: 143-44a. shook countless: many. He has said this hyperbolically, describing the monster of the dragon. "Whirlings" are the coilings of the spiral, the rotations. — And Euripides in Peirithous (fg 593 N.²): "you, the self-born, all [gods] aether with a whirl," that is, in motion, whence also the little wheel moved by sorceresses is called a "rhombus." And in Eupolis (fg 72 Kock I 274): "O rhombus, having whipped me," thus they call circular motions.
div.note: 11 Et. Gen. (AB) ῥυμβόνας: IV 144. ῥυμβόνες εἰσὶν αἱ εἱλήσεις καὶ κινήσεις τῆς σπείρας (B, πείρας A), οἱονεί· τὰς κοτυλώδεις (A, καμπυλ- B) καμπάς. ἀζαλέας τὰς σκληράς (A, ξηράς B). sch. I 1134/39 b cum loc. sim.

11 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) ῥυμβόνας: IV 144. ῥυμβόνες are the coilings and movements of the spiral (B, πείρας A), as it were the cup-like (A, curved B) bends. ἀζαλέας the hard (A, dry B). sch. I 1134/39 b with similar passages.

p.seg: ἐν τούτοις καὶ τοῖς ἐφεξῆς φησι τὴν Μήδειαν, ἐπιρραίνουσαν ἀρκεύθῳ φάρμακον, κοιμίσαι τὸν δράκοντα ἐπάδουσαν, καὶ οὕτω τὸ κῶας ἀνελέσθαι καὶ χωρισθῆναι ἀμφοτέρους ἐπὶ τὴν ναῦν κοιμωμένου τοῦ θηρίου, συμφώνως Ἀντιμάχῳ (fg 10 B. II 291). καὶ Φερεκύδης φησὶν ἐν Ζ' (3 fg 31 J.) φονευθῆναι τὸν δράκοντα ὑπὸ Ἰάσονος. ἡ δὲ ἀρκέυθος δένδρον τι ἀκανθῶδες, Ἀπόλλωνος ἴδιον, ὡς ἱστορεῖται ἐν γ' τῶν εἰς Μουσαῖον ἀναφερομένων (2 B 2 Diels-Kranz).

div.p: 156-66 a. ἡ δέ μιν ἀρκέυθ〈οιο〉: in these and the following lines he says that Medea, sprinkling the drug with juniper, put the dragon to sleep by chanting, and thus took the fleece and both departed to the ship while the beast slept, in agreement with Antimachus (fg 10 B. II 291). And Pherecydes says in the seventh book (3 fg 31 J.) that the dragon was killed by Jason. The juniper is a thorny tree, sacred to Apollo, as is recorded in the third book of the works attributed to Musaeus (2 B 2 Diels-Kranz).
div.note: 7 Et. Gen. (AB) ἄρκευθος: φυτὸν ἀκανθῶδες (A, εἶδος φυτοῦ ἀκανθώδους B), οὗ τὴν ὀδμὴν πάντα τὰ ἑρπετὰ ἀποστρέφονται. παρὰ τὸ τὴν ἀράν, ὅ ἐστι βλάβην (ὅ — βλ. A, om. B), κεύθειν· ἡ τὴν ἀρὰν κεύθουσα, ἀράκευθος καὶ ἄρκευθος. ἢ διὰ τὸ ἔχειν τὰς ἀκάνθας κεκρυμμένας. οἷον IV 156. Ἀπολλώνιος (οἷον sqq. A, om. B). Et. Gud. 197, 21 De Stef. sch. Theocr. I 133 b. c

7 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) ἄρκευθος: a thorny plant (A, a kind of thorny plant B), whose smell all reptiles avoid. From ἀρά, which is harm (ὅ — βλ. A, om. B), and κεύθειν: the one that hides harm, ἀράκευθος and ἄρκευθος. Or because it has hidden thorns. As in IV 156. Apollonius (οἷον sqq. A, om. B). Et. Gud. 197, 21 De Stef. sch. Theocr. I 133 b. c

ὁ μὲν Ἀπολλώνιος ἄπρακτόν φησιν ἀναχωρῆσαι τὸν Αἰήτην σὺν ὀχήματι ἡνιοχοῦντος Ἀψύρτου, Διονύσιος δὲ ὁ Μιλήσιος (32 fg 10 b J.) φησιν, ὅτι καταλαβὼν τὴν ναῦν ὁ Αἰήτης παραταξαμένων τῶν ἀριστέων Ἶφιν ἀνεῖλεν Ἀργεῖον, Εὐρυσθέως ἀδελφόν, καὶ αὐτὸς πολλούς ἀπέβαλε. Apollonius says that Aeetes returned without success with his chariot driven by Absyrtus, but Dionysius of Miletus (32 fr. 10b J.) says that Aeetes, overtaking the ship, when the nobles were drawn up for battle, killed Iphis the Argive, brother of Eurystheus, and lost many himself. Pherecydes in Book 7 (3 fr. 32a J.) says that Medea took him when he was small

‘οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μιᾶς
κοίτης ἔβλαστον, ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν Νηρηίδος
βλάστεσκε τέκνον ἄρτι, τὴν δ’ Εἰδυῖα πρὶν
ποτ’ Ὠκεανοῦ κόρη τέκεν.’

Absyrtus from her bed, Jason having told her, and to bring him to the Argonauts; and when they were pursued, to slaughter him and, having cut him limb from limb, to cast him into the river. But in the Scythians Sophocles says that Absyrtus was not of the same mother as Medea (fr. 546 Pearson): 'For they did not spring from one bed, but he was the child of a Nereid, just born, while her Eidyia, daughter of Oceanus, had borne before.'

p.seg: ἡ ναῦς, φησίν, βιαίᾳ ὁρμῇ τὸν πλοῦν ἤνυεν τῇ τε τῶν ἐρετῶν δυνάμει βιαζομένη καὶ τῷ τοῦ ποταμοῦ καθέλκοντι ῥεύματι.

div.p: b. The ship now with mighty: The ship, he says, was accomplishing its voyage with violent impulse, driven both by the strength of the rowers and by the current of the river drawing it down.
c. Descending: meaning 'downward-flowing'. Lg (P)

p.seg: ὁ δὲ Αἰήτης, φησίν, ἐν πολλοῖς κακοῖς γεγενημένος τὸν Ἥλιον καὶ τὸν Δία μάρτυρας τῶν πεπραγμένων ἐπεκαλεῖτο.

div.p: d. But the king in his folly: Aeetes, he says, having fallen into many misfortunes, called upon Helios and Zeus as witnesses of what had been done.

φησὶ δὲ ὁ Ἀπολλώνιος διὰ τούτων τὸν Αἰήτην ἄπρακτον ὑποστρέψαι, διὰ δὲ τῶν ἑξῆς (v. 224 sq.) φησι τὸν Ἄψυρτον νέον ὄντα ἡνιοχεῖν παραβεβηκότα τῷ πατρί. Διονύσιος δὲ ὁ Μιλήσιος (32 fg 10 a J.) φησιν, ὅτι Αἰήτης ἐδίωξεν αὐτούς· οἱ δὲ ἀριστεῖς ἠγωνίζοντο ἀκοντίζοντες, οἱ δὲ περὶ τὸν Αἰήτην ἵππευον· ἔνθα καὶ Ἶφιν τελευτῆσαι τὸν Σθενέλου· καταβαλόντα γὰρ δύο τῶν περὶ Αἰήτην ἱππέων περικατάληπτον γενέσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Αἰήτου, περισπασθέντα τῷ βρόχῳ. ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἑξῆς φησιν, ὡς οἱ Κόλχοι εἰς φυγὴν ἐτράπησαν. Φερεκύδης δὲ ἐν Ζ (3 fg 32 b J.) διωκομένους ἀναβιβάσαι ἐπὶ τὴν ναῦν τὸν Ἄψυρτον καὶ μελίσαντας ῥῖψαι εἰς τὸν ποταμόν. Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ἐν Κολχίσι (fg 343 Pearson) φησι κατὰ τὸν οἶκον τοῦ Αἰήτου τὸν παῖδα σφαγῆναι. ἑξῆς δὲ Ἀπολλώνιος τὴν ἀπειλὴν τάσσει τὴν πρὸς τοὺς Κόλχους.

Apollonius says through these lines that Aeetes returned without success, and through the following lines (v. 224 ff.) he says that Absyrtus, being young, rode as charioteer beside his father. But Dionysius of Miletus (32 fr. 10a J.) says that Aeetes pursued them; the chiefs fought by hurling javelins, while those around Aeetes rode on horseback; there Iphis, son of Sthenelus, also died; for after striking down two of the horsemen around Aeetes, he was surrounded by Aeetes and dragged off with a noose. In the following lines he says that the Colchians turned to flight. Pherecydes in Book 7 (3 fr. 32b J.) says that when they were pursued, they brought Absyrtus onto the ship, cut him limb from limb, and threw him into the river. Sophocles in the Colchian Women (fr. 343 Pearson) says that the boy was slaughtered in the house of Aeetes. Next Apollonius places the threat against the Colchians.

p.seg: 247—52. καὶ δὴ τὰ μέν, ὅσσα θυηλ〈ή〉:

ἐκ τούτου βούλεται δηλῶσαι, ὅτι τοιαύτην θυσίαν ἐβούλετο τελέσαι ὁποίαν φαρμακίδες. Νύμφις δὲ ἐν τῷ ς' Περὶ Ἡρακλείας (fg 14 M. III 15) Ἑκάτης φησὶν ἱερὸν εἶναι ἐν τῇ Παφλαγονίᾳ Μηδείας ἱδρυσαμένης. κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἀποσιώπησιν ἐμφάσει κέχρηται, τὴν ταῖς φαρμακίσι τελουμένην θυσίαν μὴ ἐξεργαζόμενος.

div.p: 247-52. And indeed all that with sacrifice: From this he wishes to make clear that she intended to perform such a sacrifice as sorceresses do. Nymphis in the sixth book of his work On Heraclea (fr. 14 M. III 15) says that there is a sanctuary of Hecate in Paphlagonia founded by Medea. By the aposiopesis he employs emphasis, not elaborating on the sacrifice performed by sorceresses.

p.seg: διὰ τούτων φησὶν ὁ Ἄργος ἀληθῆ αὐτοῖς εἰρῆσθαι ὑπὸ Φινέως (II 421)· εἶναι γὰρ πλοῦν ἕτερον ἔξω φέροντα, ὃν Αἰγύπτιοι ἱερεῖς ἐσημήναντο. ἐγίνωσκε γὰρ τὰ μέρη ἐκεῖνα ὁ Ἄργος. διό φησιν· ὄντως δὴ τῇ ἐσωτάτῃ ὁδῷ κεχρημένοι, ᾗ καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς Ὀρχομενὸν ἐπορευόμεθα, πορεύεσθε. L

div.p: 257-62a. We are going to Orchomenus: through these words Argus says that the things told to them by Phineus (II 421) were true; for there is another voyage leading outside, which the Egyptian priests indicated. For Argus knew those regions. Therefore he says: 'Indeed, having used the innermost route, by which we also were traveling to Orchomenus, proceed.' L

p.seg: Ἡρόδωρος ἐν τοῖς Ἀργοναύταις (31 fg 10 J.) φησὶ διὰ τῆς αὐτῆς 〈κατ〉ελθεῖν θαλάσσης, δι’ ἧς ἦλθον εἰς Κόλχους. Ἑκαταῖος δὲ ὁ Μιλήσιος (1 fg 18 a J.) ἐκ τοῦ Φάσιδος διελθεῖν εἰς τὸν ὠκεανόν, εἶτα ἐκεῖθεν εἰς τὸν Νεῖλον, ὅθεν εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν θάλασσαν. τοῦτο δὲ ὁ Ἐφέσιος Ἀρτεμίδωρος (fg 136 Stiehle Phil. 11, 1856, 236) ψεῦδός φησιν εἶναι· τὸν γὰρ Φάσιν μὴ συμβάλλειν τῷ ὠκεανῷ, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ὀρέων καταφέρεσθαι. τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ Ἐρατοσθένης ἐν γ' Γεωγραφικῶν (fg III B 74 Berger) φησι. Τιμάγητος δὲ ἐν α' Περὶ λιμένων (fg 1 M. IV 519) τὸν μὲν Φᾶσιν 〈καταφέρεσθαι . . ., τὸν δὲ Ἴστρον〉 καταφέρεσθαι ἐκ τῶν †Κελτικῶν† ὀρῶν, ἅ ἐστι τῆς Κελτικῆς, εἶτα ἐκδιδόναι εἰς Κελτῶν λίμνην, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα εἰς δύο σχίζεσθαι τὸ ὕδωρ, καὶ τὸ μὲν εἰς τὸν Εὔξεινον πόντον εἰσβάλλειν, τὸ δὲ εἰς τὴν †Κελτικήν† θάλασσαν· διὰ δὲ τούτου τοῦ στόματος πλεῦσαι τοὺς Ἀργοναύτας καὶ ἐλθεῖν εἰς Τυρρηνίαν. κατακολουθεῖ δὲ αὐτῷ καὶ Ἀπολλώνιος. Ἡσίοδος (fg 64 Rz.²) δὲ καὶ Πίνδαρος ἐν Πυθιονίκαις

div.p: b. For there is another voyage: Herodorus in his Argonautica (31 fr. 10 J.) says that they came down through the same sea by which they went to Colchis. Hecataeus of Miletus (1 fr. 18a J.) says that they passed from the Phasis into the ocean, then from there into the Nile, and from there into our sea. Artemidorus of Ephesus (fr. 136 Stiehle Phil. 11, 1856, 236) says this is false; for the Phasis does not join the ocean, but flows down from mountains. Eratosthenes in the third book of his Geography (fr. III B 74 Berger) says the same. Timagetus in the first book of On Harbours (fr. 1 M. IV 519) says that the Phasis flows down from the †Celtic† mountains, which are in Celtica, then empties into the Celtic lake, and after this the water divides into two, and one part flows into the Euxine Sea, the other into the †Celtic† sea; and through this mouth the Argonauts sailed and came to Tyrrhenia. Apollonius follows him. Hesiod (fr. 64 Rz.²) and Pindar in his Pythian odes

(IV 25 sq.) and Antimachus in his Lyde (fr. 12 B. II 291) say that they came through the ocean to Libya, and carrying the Argo into our sea they arrived.

p.seg: τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους πολλοὶ παλαιοτάτους εἶναί φασιν, Ἡρόδοτος (II 2) δὲ Φρύγας. Μύσημης δὲ ἐν α' Αἰγυπτιακῶν (M. IV 369) καὶ Λέων ἐν α' τῶν Πρὸς τὴν μητέρα (fg 1 M. II 331) καὶ Κνωσσὸς ἐν α' Γεωγραφικῶν τῆς Ἀσίας (M. III 158) πάντων ἀρχαιοτάτους Αἰγυπτίους εἶναί φασιν.

div.p: c. Not yet of the Danaans: many say that the Egyptians are the most ancient, but Herodotus (II 2) says the Phrygians. Mysemes in the first book of his Aegyptiaca (M. IV 369) and Leon in the first book of his work Against his Mother (fr. 1 M. II 331) and Cnossus in the first book of his Geography of Asia (M. III 158) say that the Egyptians are the most ancient of all.

δοκεῖ δὲ πρῶτον Θήβην κατ’ Αἴγυπτον κτισθῆναι, ὡς φησι Ξεναγόρας ἐν α' Χρόνων (240 fg 1 J.). καὶ Νικάνωρ δὲ λέγει ἐν ταῖς Μετονομασίαις (fg 15 M. III 634) ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ πρώτην κτισθῆναι πόλιν Θήβας, καὶ αὐτὸς συμφωνῶν τῷ Ἀρχεμάχῳ (fg 6 M. IV 315).

It seems that Thebes in Egypt was founded first, as Xenagoras says in Book 1 of his Chronicles (240 FGrH 1 J.). And Nicanor also says in his Renamings (FGrH 15 M. III 634) that the city of Thebes was founded first in Egypt, himself agreeing with Archemachus (FGrH 6 M. IV 315).

Ἵππυς (fg 1 M. II 13) δὲ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους πρώτους 〈γεγενῆσθαι〉 στοχάζεται 〈ἐκ〉 τῆς τοῦ ἀέρος κράσεως καὶ 〈ἐκ τοῦ〉 γονιμώτατον εἶναι τὸ τοῦ Νείλου ὕδωρ. γεγονέναι δὲ αὐτούς φησιν ὁ Ἀπολλώνιος πρὸ τοῦ πάντα τὰ ἄστρα φανῆναι· καθὸ τήν τε φύσιν κατανοῆσαι αὐτῶν δοκοῦσι καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα θεῖναι, 〈καὶ〉 τὰ μὲν ιβ' ζῴδια θεοὺς βουλαίους προσηγόρευον, τοὺς δὲ πλάνητας ῥαβδοφόρους.

Hippys (FGrH 1 M. II 13) conjectures that the Egyptians were the first to come into being from the temperament of the air and from the fact that the water of the Nile is most productive. Apollonius says that they existed before all the stars appeared; for which reason they are thought to have observed their nature and given them names, and they called the twelve zodiac signs "counselor gods," and the planets "rod-bearers."

Ἡρόδοτος (l. l.) δέ φησι Φρύγας πρώτους γεγενῆσθαι. ὕστερον δὲ Ψαμμίτιχος τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλεύς, βουλόμενος διαγνῶναι, τίνες οἱ γηγενεῖς, παρέδωκεν ποιμένι δύο βρέφη, κελεύσας μηδένα φθέγγεσθαι, μόνον δὲ αὐτοῖς αἰγὸς θηλὴν δίδοσθαι. οἱ δὲ δύο ἐτῶν διελθόντων

Herodotus (loc. cit.) says that the Phrygians were the first to come into being. Later Psammetichus, king of the Egyptians, wishing to determine who were the earth-born, handed over two infants to a shepherd, ordering that no one speak, but only that a goat's teat be given to them. After two years had passed,

div.p: πρώτην φωνὴν ἀφῆκαν τὸ βέκος· οὕτω δὲ λέγεται παρὰ τοῖς Φρυξὶν ὁ ἄρτος. ἐγνώσθησαν οὖν ἀπὸ τούτου οἱ Φρύγες γηγενεῖς. οἱ δέ φασιν, ὅτι εὔηθές ἐστιν ὑπολαμβάνειν τοῦτο· ἀκούοντες γὰρ οἱ παῖδες βληχωμένων τῶν προβάτων, ὡς ἂν ὑπὸ τῆς φύσεως ἐνεργούμενοι πρὸς τὸ ἔναρθρον τὴν φωνὴν ἀπέστρεψαν.

they uttered as their first word "bekos"; for thus bread is called among the Phrygians. From this, then, the Phrygians were recognized as earth-born. But others say that it is foolish to suppose this; for the children, hearing the sheep bleating, as if moved by nature toward articulate speech, turned their voice to that.

p.seg: μόνοι δὲ ἦσαν Ἀρκάδες, φησί, τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἀρχαιότεροι. Ἀπιδανῆας δὲ τοὺς Πελοποννησίους ἀπὸ Ἄπιδος τοῦ Φορωνέως.

div.p: 263-64a. "Such as the Arcadians were": The Arcadians alone, he says, were older than the Greeks. "Apidaneans" refers to the Peloponnesians, from Apis son of Phoroneus.

p.seg: οἱ Ἀρκάδες δοκοῦσι πρὸ τῆς σελήνης γεγονέναι, ὡς καὶ Εὔδοξος ἐν Γῆς περιόδῳ (fg 41 Brandes). Θεόδωρος δὲ ἐν κβ' (62 fg 2 J.) ὀλίγῳ πρότερόν φησι τοῦ πρὸς τοὺς Γίγαντας πολέμου Ἡρακλέους τὴν σελήνην φανῆναι. καὶ Ἀριστίας ὁ Χῖος ἐν ταῖς Κτίσεσι καὶ Διονύσιος ὁ Χαλκιδεὺς ἐν α' Κτίσεων (fg 1 M. IV 393) καὶ ἔθνος φασὶν Ἀρκαδίας Σεληνίτας εἶναι. — Μνασέας (fg 4 M. III 150) δέ φησι Προσέληνον Ἀρκάδων βασιλεῦσαι. Ἀριστοτέλης δὲ ἐν τῇ Τεγεατῶν πολιτείᾳ (fg 549 Rose 1568b 41) φησίν, ὅτι βάρβαροι τὴν Ἀρκαδίαν ᾤκησαν, οἵτινες ἐξεβλήθησαν ὑπὸ τῶν νῦν Ἀρκάδων, ἐπιθεμένων αὐτοῖς πρὸ τοῦ ἐπιτεῖλαι τὴν σελήνην· διὸ κατωνομάσθησαν προσέληνοι. 〈...〉. Δοῦρις δὲ ἐν ιε' τῶν Μακεδονικῶν (76 fg 9 J.) Ἀρκάδα φησίν, ἀφ’ οὗ ἡ Ἀρκαδία καλεῖται, Ὀρχομενοῦ υἱόν, διὸ καὶ πόλιν τῆς Ἀρκαδίας Ὀρχομενόν. τινὲς δέ φασιν Ἐνδυμίωνα εὑρηκέναι τὰς περιόδους καὶ τοὺς ἀριθμοὺς τῆς σελήνης, ὅθεν καὶ προσελήνους τοὺς Ἀρκάδας κληθῆναι. ἔνιοι δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ Τυφῶνος 〈...〉· ὑπὸ δὲ Ἄτλαντος καὶ Ξεναγόρας (240 fg 32 J.) εἴρηκεν.

div.p: b. Arcadians, who even before: The Arcadians are thought to have existed before the moon, as Eudoxus also says in his Circuit of the Earth (fr. 41 Brandes). Theodorus in his twenty-second book (62 fr. 2 J.) says that the moon appeared a little before Heracles' war against the Giants. And Aristias of Chios in his Foundations and Dionysius of Chalcis in the first book of his Foundations (fr. 1 M. IV 393) say that there is also a people of Arcadia called Selenitae. — Mnaseas (fr. 4 M. III 150) says that Proselenus ruled over the Arcadians. Aristotle in his Constitution of the Tegeans (fr. 549 Rose 1568b 41) says that barbarians inhabited Arcadia, who were expelled by the present Arcadians, who attacked them before the moon rose; for this reason they were called proselenoi. 〈...〉. Duris in the fifteenth book of his Macedonian History (76 fr. 9 J.) says that Arcas, from whom Arcadia is named, was the son of Orchomenus, and for this reason there is also a city of Arcadia called Orchomenus. Some say that Endymion discovered the circuits and numbers of the moon, whence the Arcadians were also called proselenoi. Others say that by Typhon 〈...〉; and by Atlas, as Xenagoras (240 fr. 32 J.) has said.

div.p: 265-66. ruled over the Deucalionids: Those who trace their lineage from Deucalion ruled Thessaly, as Hecataeus (1 fr. 14 J.) and Hesiod (fr. 8 Rz.²) say. Thessaly was called Pelasgis after Pelasgus, who was its king.

p.seg:
περὶ τῆς τοῦ Νείλου ἀναδόσεως διάφοροι αἰτίαι παρὰ τοῖς παλαιοῖς ἐλέγοντο. Ἀναξαγόρας (cf. 59 A 91 Diels-Kranz) μὲν γάρ φησι διὰ τῆξιν τῆς χιόνος πληθύειν αὐτόν· ᾧ ἕπεται καὶ Εὐριπίδης λέγων (Hel. 1. 3)·
‘Νείλου μὲν αἵδε καλλιπάρθενοι ῥοαί,
λευκῆς τακείσης χιόνος ὑγραίνει γύην.’
καὶ Αἰσχύλος (fg 300 N.²) δὲ καὶ Σοφοκλῆς (fg 882 Pearson) ὑπέλαβον τοὺς ὑπὲρ τὴν Αἴγυπτον χιονίζεσθαι τόπους καὶ τηκομένης τῆς χιόνος τὴν χύσιν εἰς τὸν Νεῖλον ἐκδίδοσθαι. Νικαγόρας (M. II 332 b) δέ φησιν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀντοίκων αὐτὸν ῥεῖν. Δημόκριτος δὲ ὁ φυσικὸς (68 A 99 Diels-Kranz) ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ μεσημβρίαν ὑπερκειμένου πελάγους λαμβάνειν τὸν Νεῖλον τὴν ἐπίχυσιν, ἀπογλυκαίνεσθαι δὲ τὸ ὕδωρ διὰ τὸ διάστημα καὶ τὸ μῆκος τοῦ πόρου καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ καύματος ἀφεψόμενον· διὸ καὶ ἐναντίαν φησὶν ἔχειν τὴν γεῦσιν. Οἰνοπίδης δὲ ὁ Χῖος (cf. 41, 11 Diels-Kranz), ὅτι χειμῶνος ὢν ὑπὸ γῆν ὁ ἥλιος ἐκπέμπει τὸ ὕδωρ, τοῦ δὲ θέρους γενόμενος ὑπὲρ γῆν οὐκέτι διὰ τὸ μᾶλλον θερμαίνεσθαι αὐτήν· διὸ κεχαραδρωμένη ἡ γῆ πλεῖον ὕδωρ ἀναδίδωσιν.

div.p: 269-71a. and the river Triton: Various causes for the rising of the Nile were given by the ancients. Anaxagoras (cf. 59 A 91 Diels-Kranz) says that it swells because of the melting of snow; Euripides follows him, saying (Hel. 1.3): 'These fair-maidened streams of the Nile, from white snow melted, moisten the land.' And Aeschylus (fg 300 N.²) and Sophocles (fg 882 Pearson) supposed that the regions above Egypt are snow-covered and that from the melting snow the flow is discharged into the Nile. Nicagoras (M. II 332 b) says that it flows from the inhabitants of the opposite region. Democritus the natural philosopher (68 A 99 Diels-Kranz) says that the Nile receives its influx from the sea lying to the south above it, and that the water is made sweet by the distance and length of the passage and by being boiled off by the heat; therefore he says it has the opposite taste. Oenopides of Chios (cf. 41, 11 Diels-Kranz), because in winter the sun is under the earth and sends out the water, but in summer it is above the earth and no longer does so because the earth is heated more; therefore the earth, being full of gullies, gives forth more water.
div.note: 5 267. Et. Gen. (AB) Ἠερία: ἡ Αἴγυπτος τὸ πρὶν ἐκαλεῖτο — Ἀπολλώνιος· IV 267—268 —, ὅτι τοῖς ἐπ’ αὐτὴν πλέουσι (B, αὐτῆς κλαίουσι A) κοιλὴ οὖσα οὐ φαίνεται πρὶν ἂν σχεδὸν ὁρμισθῶσι, (Et. M., -ηθῶσι AB) καὶ τότε ὥσπερ ἐξ ὁμίχλης καὶ (καὶ B, om. A) ἀέρος κεκαλυμμένη φαίνεται. sch. I 580 a cum loc. sim. cf. W 81 Ps.-Arist. De inund. Nili Rose 1863, 633—39 Diod. I 38—41 Sen. Nat. Quaest. Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) Ἠερία: Egypt was formerly called Ἠερία — Apollonius: IV 267—268 —, because to those sailing to it (B, to those weeping for it A) being hollow it is not visible until they are almost anchored, (Et. div.p: Ἔφορος (70 fg 65 d J.) δὲ ποταμόχωστον εἶναί φησι τὴν Αἴγυπτον, ῥηγνυμένης δὲ τῆς γῆς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τῷ ἔαρι ἀναπηδᾶν τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ ἐπαύξεσθαι τὸ ῥεῦμα. Θαλῆς δὲ ὁ Μιλήσιος (cf. 11 A 16 Diels-Kranz) φησιν ὑπὸ τῶν ἐτησίων συνελαυνόμενα τὰ νέφη κατὰ τὰ ὄρη τῆς Αἰθιοπίας αὐτόθι ῥήγνυσθαι· ὅταν δὲ τοῦ ποταμοῦ ἐξεναντίας συστῶσιν αἱ πνοαὶ προσπίπτουσαι τῇ θαλάσσῃ, ἐκ τῆς ἀποπεμπομένης πλήσμης τὰς ὑπερχύσεις ἀναδέχεσθαι τὸν Νεῖλον. Διογένης δὲ ὁ Ἀπολλωνιάτης (64 A 18 Diels-Kranz) ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου ἁρπάζεσθαι τὸ ὕδωρ τῆς θαλάσσης, ὃ τότε εἰς τὸν Νεῖλον καταφέρεσθαι· οἴεται γὰρ πληροῦσθαι τὸν Νεῖλον ἐν τῷ θέρει διὰ τὸ τὸν ἥλιον εἰς τοῦτον τὰς ἀπὸ γῆς ἰκμάδας τρέπειν.

Ephorus (70 fg 65 d J.) says that Egypt is alluvial, and that when the earth is broken open by the sun in spring the water springs up and the stream increases. Thales of Miletus (cf. 11 A 16 Diels-Kranz) says that the clouds are driven together by the Etesian winds against the mountains of Ethiopia and burst there; and when the winds blowing against the river strike the sea, the Nile receives its overflow from the flood that is driven back. Diogenes of Apollonia (64 A 18 Diels-Kranz) says that the water of the sea is snatched up by the sun, which then is carried down into the Nile; for he thinks that the Nile is filled in summer because the sun turns the moisture from the earth into it.
ὁ δὲ Νεῖλος οὕτω τὸ πρότερον ἐκαλεῖτο, Τρίτων. μετωνομάσθη δὲ ἀπὸ Νείλου τοῦ Κύκλωπος τοῦ Ταντάλου, βασιλεύσαντος τῆς χώρας, ὡς Ἕρμιππός (fg 77 M. III 53) φησιν.
The Nile was formerly called Triton. It was renamed after Neilos, the Cyclops, son of Tantalus, who was king of the country, as Hermippus (fr. 77 M. III 53) says.

div.p: b. Rain in abundance: ambiguity in the construction. For it means either "they sprout in abundance" or "rain does not wet abundantly," since it does not rain continuously in Egypt.

p.seg: Σεσόγχωσις Αἰγύπτου πάσης βασιλεὺς μετὰ Ὦρον τὸν Ἴσιδος καὶ Ὀσίριδος παῖδα τὴν μὲν Ἀσίαν ὁρμήσας πᾶσαν κατεστρέψατο, ὁμοίως καὶ τὰ πλεῖστα τῆς Εὐρώπης. ἀκριβέστερον δὲ ἔστι τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ παρὰ Ἡροδότῳ (II 102—10). Θεόπομπος δὲ ἐν γ' (115 fg 46 J.) Σέσωστριν αὐτὸν καλεῖ. Ἡρόδοτος δὲ προστίθησιν (102), ὅτι, εἰ μέν τινας πολέμῳ κατέστρεψεν, στήλας ἐτίθει πῶς ἐνίκησεν· εἰ δὲ παρεχώρουν, γυναικεῖον ταῖς στήλαις αἰδοῖον προσετίθει σύμβολον τῆς μαλακίας. Δικαίαρχος δὲ ἐν α' Ἑλλάδος βίου (fg 7 M. II 235) Σεσόγχωσιν καὶ νόμους [αὐτὸν] θεῖναι λέγει, ὥστε μηδένα

div.p: 272-74. From there indeed some: Sesonchosis, king of all Egypt after Horus, the son of Isis and Osiris, set out and subdued all Asia, and likewise most of Europe. More accurate accounts about him are in Herodotus (II 102-10). Theopompus in the third book (115 fr. 46 J.) calls him Sesostris. Herodotus adds (102) that if he subdued any peoples in war, he set up pillars recording how he conquered; but if they yielded, he added to the pillars a female genital as a symbol of their softness. Dicaearchus in the first book of the Life of Greece (fr. 7 M. II 235) says that Sesonchosis also established laws, so that no one

div.p: καταλιπεῖν τὴν πατρώαν τέχνην· τοῦτο γὰρ ὑπολαμβάνειν ἀρχὴν εἶναι πλεονεξίας. καὶ πρῶτόν φησιν αὐτὸν εὑρηκέναι ἵππων ἄνθρωπον ἐπιβαίνειν· οἱ δὲ ταῦτα τὸν Ὦρον, οὐ τὸν Σεσόγχωσιν.

to abandon their ancestral craft; for this he supposed to be the beginning of greed. And he says that he was the first to discover a man riding on horses; but others attribute these things to Horus, not to Sesonchosis.

p.seg: 276. ἠὲ καὶ οὐ· πουλὺς γὰρ ἄδην:

ἢ γὰρ ἐκλελοίπασι τινες τῶν πόλεων κἂν μετονομασμέναι [καὶ] ἀγνοοῦνται, ὑφ’ οὗ τυγχάνουσιν ἐκτισμέναι· τούτου δὲ τὸν χρόνον αἴτιον γεγενῆσθαι. περὶ δὲ τῶν χρόνων, καθ’ οὓς ἐγένετο Σεσόγχωσις, ὁ μὲν Ἀπολλώνιός φησι πουλὺς γὰρ ἄδην ἐπενήνοθεν αἰών, Δικαίαρχος δὲ ἐν α' (v. sch. 272/74) μετὰ τὸν Ἴσιδος καὶ Ὀσίριδος Ὦρον βασιλέα γεγονέναι Σεσόγχωσιν. γίνεται δὲ ἀπὸ Σεσογχώσεως ἐπὶ τὴν Νείλου βασιλείαν ἔτη ,βφ', 〈ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Νείλου βασιλείας ἐπὶ τὴν Ἰλίου ἅλωσιν Ζ',〉 ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Ἰλίου ἁλώσεως ἐπὶ τὴν α' Ὀλυμπιάδα υλγ', ὁμοῦ ,βϠμγ'.

div.p: 276. Or even not; for abundant enough: For either some of the cities have been abandoned and, having been renamed, are unknown, by whom they happen to have been founded; and time has been the cause of this. Concerning the times in which Sesonchosis lived, Apollonius says "for abundant enough time has passed," but Dicaearchus in the first book (see sch. 272/74) says that Sesonchosis was king after Horus, the son of Isis and Osiris. From Sesonchosis to the reign of Neilos is 2,500 years, <from the reign of Neilos to the capture of Troy 7,> from the capture of Troy to the first Olympiad 433, in total 2,943.

τὴν Αἰάν φησιν ἀπὸ τῶν Σεσογχώσεως χρόνων μέχρις αὐτοῦ μένειν ἄθραυστον καὶ τοὺς ἐκείνων ἀπογόνους τῶν ὑπὸ Σεσογχώσεως κατοικισθέντων. τούτους γὰρ υἱωνοὺς εἴρηκε καταχρηστικῶς, ὡς Ἡρακλεῖδαι λέγονται οὐ μόνον οἱ Ἡρακλέους παῖδες, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ ἐκείνων ἀπόγονοι. οὕτως καὶ οἱ ἐν τῇ Σκυθίᾳ ἀπόγονοι τῶν Αἰγυπτίων εἰσίν, ὡς καὶ Ἀπολλώνιος. καὶ Σκύμνος φησὶν ἐν Ἀσίᾳ, ὅτι Κόλχοι Αἰγυπτίων ἄποικοι. καὶ Ἡρόδωρος ἐν β' (104 sq.) μέμνηται τῆς περιτομῆς τῶν μορίων καὶ τῆς τῶν λίνων ὑφῆς, καὶ νόμοις αὐτούς φησι κεχρῆσθαι τῶν Αἰγυπτίων.

div.p: 277-78a. Aea at least even now remains: He says that Aea has remained unbroken from the time of Sesonchosis until his own day, and that those descendants are of the people settled by Sesonchosis. For he has called these 'grandsons' loosely, just as Heracleidae are called not only the children of Heracles, but also their descendants. Thus also those in Scythia are descendants of the Egyptians, as Apollonius too says. And Scymnus says in his work on Asia that the Colchians are colonists of the Egyptians. And Herodorus in Book 2 (104 sq.) mentions the circumcision of their private parts and the weaving of linen, and says that they use the customs of the Egyptians.

div.p: 279-81a. They indeed with painted tablets: There are, he says, among them also laws of their ancestors and pillars, on which are inscribed records of land and sea.

p.seg: στήλας. λέγει δὲ τοὺς ἄξονας, ἐν οἷς οἱ νόμοι γράφονται, ὡς Ἀριστοφάνης ὁ κωμικός (Αν. 1354). Ἀπολλόδωρος (244 fg 107 b J.) δέ φησι πᾶσαν δημοσίαν γραφὴν καὶ νόμους κύρβιν καλεῖσθαι, ὅτι οἱ ἀρχαίοι λίθους ἱστάντες τὸ δόξαν ἀνέγραφον, οὓς μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς στάσεως στήλας, κύρβεις δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς εἰς ὕψος ἀνατάσεως διὰ τὸ ἀπο〈κεκορυφῶσθαι〉, [ἢ] οἷον κύρφεις. ὕστερον δὲ 〈εἰς〉 ξύλα λελευκωμένα γράφοντες ὁμοίως ἐκάλεσαν. κύρβις οὖν ἡ περιέχουσα τὰς ἱερὰς ἀναγραφάς ἐστιν.

div.p: b. kyrbeis: pillars. He means the axones, on which the laws are written, as the comic poet Aristophanes (Birds 1354). But Apollodorus (244 F 107b J.) says that every public writing and laws are called a kyrbis, because the ancients, setting up stones, inscribed what had been decided, calling them stelae from their standing, and kyrbeis from their rising to a height because of being topped off, as it were kyrpheis. Later, writing on whitened wooden tablets, they called them the same. A kyrbis, then, is that which contains the sacred records.

p.seg: κύρβεις λέγουσιν, ὡς Ἐρατοσθένης (fg 80 Strecker = 241 fg 37 a J.), τοὺς ἄξονας καλουμένους Ἀθήνησιν, ἐν οἷς οἱ νόμοι περιέχονται. οἱ δὲ ἀκριβέστεροι ἄξονας μὲν τετραγώνους λίθους, κύρβεις δὲ τριγώνους· ἐν ἀμφοτέροις δὲ νόμοι ἦσαν γεγραμμένοι Ἀθήνησι. ἐνταῦθα δὲ κύρβιάς φησι πίνακάς τινας γῆς περίοδον περιέχοντας.

div.p: c. κύρβιας: They call κύρβεις, as Eratosthenes (fg 80 Strecker = 241 fg 37 a J.) says, the so-called ἄξονες at Athens, in which the laws are contained. But the more precise authorities say that ἄξονες are quadrangular stones, while κύρβεις are triangular; on both, laws were written at Athens. Here, however, he says κύρβιας, meaning certain tablets containing a description of the earth.

div.p: 282-91 a. κέρας ὠκεανοῖο: They call 'horns of Ocean' all the rivers that flow down from it. The Ister is a river of Scythia. The sense: from afar they discerned the river and recognized it.

τὸν Ἴστρον φησὶν ἐκ τῶν Ὑπερβορέων καταφέρεσθαι καὶ τῶν Ῥιπαίων ὀρῶν· γενόμενον δὲ μεταξὺ Σκυθῶν καὶ Θρακῶν σχίζεσθαι, καὶ τὸ μὲν εἰς τὴν καθ’ ἡμᾶς θάλασσαν ἐκβάλλειν ῥεῖθρον, τὸ δὲ εἰς τὴν Ποντικὴν θάλασσαν ἐκτίπτειν [τὸ δὲ εἰς τὸν Ἀδριατικὸν κόλπον]. οὕτω δὲ εἶπεν ἀκολουθῶν Αἰσχύλῳ, ἐν Λυομένῳ Προμηθεῖ (fg 197 N.²) λέγοντι τοῦτο. Ῥίπαια δὲ ὄρη πρὸς ταῖς ἀνατολαῖς, ὡς Καλλίμαχος (fg 215 Schn.)·
‘Ῥιπαίου πέμπουσιν ἀπ’ οὔρεος, ἦχι μάλιστα.’
Ἐρατοσθένης δὲ ἐν γ' Γεωγραφικῶν (fg III B 99 Berger) ἐξ ἐρήμων τόπων ῥεῖν, περιβάλλειν δὲ νῆσον Πεύκην. Σκύμνος δὲ ἐν τῇ [ι]ς' Περὶ Εὐρώπης αὐτὸ μόνον φησίν, ἀπὸ ἐρήμων φέρεσθαι τὸν Ἴστρον.

div.p: b. Ἴστρον μιν καλέ〈οντες〉: He says that the Ister flows down from the Hyperboreans and the Rhipaean mountains; and when it comes between the Scythians and Thracians it divides, and one stream flows into our sea, while the other falls into the Pontic sea [and the other into the Adriatic gulf]. He said this following Aeschylus, who says this in the Prometheus Unbound (fg 197 N.²). The Rhipaean mountains are toward the east, as Callimachus (fg 215 Schn.) says: 'from the Rhipaean mountain they send, where especially...' Eratosthenes in the third book of his Geography (fg III B 99 Berger) says that it flows from desert places and encircles the island of Peuce. Scymnus in the sixteenth book of his On Europe says only this, that the Ister is borne from desert places.

οὐδεὶς δὲ ἱστορεῖ διὰ τούτου τοὺς Ἀργοναύτας εἰσπεπλευκέναι εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν θάλασσαν ἔξω Τιμαγήτου (fg 1 M. IV 519), ᾧ ἠκολούθησεν Ἀπολλώνιος. ὁ μὲν γὰρ Σκύμνος αὐτοὺς διὰ Τανάιδος πεπλευκέναι ἐπὶ τὴν μεγάλην θάλασσαν, ἐκεῖθεν δὲ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν θάλασσαν ἐληλυθέναι. καὶ παρεκβολεύεται, ὡς ἄρα ἐλθόντες ἐπὶ τὴν ἤπειρον οἱ Ἀργοναῦται ἐπὶ στρωτήρων ἐκόμισαν τὴν Ἀργώ, μέχρις οὗ ἐπὶ θάλασσαν

No one records that the Argonauts sailed through this river into our sea except Timagetus (fg 1 M. IV 519), whom Apollonius followed. For Scymnus says that they sailed through the Tanais to the great sea, and from there came to our sea. And he adds the digression that the Argonauts, having come to the mainland, carried the Argo on rollers until they reached the sea.

p.seg: Ἡσίοδος (fg 65 Rz.?) δὲ διὰ Φάσιδος αὐτοὺς εἰσπεπλευκέναι λέγει. Ἑκαταῖος (1 fg 18b J.) δὲ 〈. . . Ἀρτεμίδωρος (v. sch. 257/62 b) δὲ〉 ἐλέγχων αὐτὸν ἱστορεῖ μὴ ἐκδιδόναι εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν τὸν Φᾶσιν. οὐδὲ διὰ Τανάιδος ἔπλευσαν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν πλοῦν, καθ’ ὃν καὶ πρότερον, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς ἐν Σκύθαις (fg 547 Pearson) ἱστορεῖ καὶ Καλλίμαχος (fg 377 Schn.). 〈. . .〉 αὐτῶν τοὺς μὲν εἰς τὸν Ἀδρίαν πεπλευκότας μὴ εὑρεῖν τοὺς Ἀργοναύτας, τοὺς δὲ διὰ τῶν Κυανέων πετρῶν ἐπὶ τὴν Κέρκυραν, ἔνθα κἀκεῖνοι τότε ἦσαν.

div.p: They arrived. Hesiod (fr. 65 Rz.?) says that they sailed in through the Phasis. Hecataeus (1 fr. 18b J.) 〈... Artemidorus (see schol. 257/62b)〉 refuting him records that the Phasis does not flow out into the sea. Nor did they sail through the Tanais, but by the same route as before, as Sophocles in the Scythians (fr. 547 Pearson) records and Callimachus (fr. 377 Schn.). 〈...〉 of them, those who had sailed into the Adriatic did not find the Argonauts, but those who went through the Cyanean rocks to Corcyra, where they then were.

ὁ δὲ Ἴστρος καταφερόμενος ἐξ Ὑπερβορέων, ὅταν φθάσῃ ἐπὶ τὸν μεταξὺ Σκυθίας καὶ Θράκης τόπον, σχίζεται εἰς δύο, καὶ τὸ μὲν αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν Εὔξεινον πόντον βάλλει, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον εἰς τὴν Τρινακρίαν θάλασσαν.

The Ister, flowing down from the Hyperboreans, when it reaches the region between Scythia and Thrace, splits into two, and one part of it empties into the Euxine Sea, the other into the Trinacrian sea.
c. μορμύρουσιν: they roar. Lᶢ P

p.seg: παράκειται τῇ Σικελίᾳ· ἐκαλεῖτο γὰρ Τρινακρία τὸ πρότερον διὰ τὸ τρεῖς ἄκρας ἔχειν, Πάχυνον, Λιλύβαιον, Πέλωρον. Lᵐ P

div.p: d. The Trinacrian sea lies adjacent to Sicily; for it was formerly called Trinacria because it has three headlands, Pachynus, Lilybaeum, Pelorus. Lᵐ P

p.seg: ἐὰν μὲν οὕτω γράφηται γαίῃ ὅς ὑμετέρῃ, ἔσται τῇ Ἑλλάδι· τὸ γὰρ Τρινάκριον πέλαγος παράκειται τῇ τῶν Ἑλλήνων γῇ. ἐὰν δὲ ἡμετέρῃ, ἔσται ὁ Ἴστρος· παράκειται γὰρ τοῖς Κόλχοις οὗτος.

div.p: 292-93a. γαίῃ ὅς ὑμετέρῃ: if it is written thus, γαίῃ ὅς ὑμετέρῃ, it will mean Hellas; for the Trinacrian sea lies adjacent to the land of the Greeks. But if it is ἡμετέρῃ, it will be the Ister; for this lies adjacent to the Colchians.

div.note: 15 sch. 965 sch. λ 107 sch. Nic. Ther. 529 sch. Lyc. 966 Strab. VI 265 Steph. Byz. Τρινακρία — Eust. Dion. Per. 467

p.seg: ὁ Ἀχελῷος τῶν τῆς Ἑλλάδος ποταμῶν τῶν ἄλλων διαπρεπέστατος.

div.p: b. ὑμετέρης γαίης: the Achelous is the most distinguished of the other rivers of Hellas.
εἰ οὖν ἄρα ὁ Ἀχελῷος παρ’ ὑμῖν ἐστιν· τὸ γὰρ ὄνομα ἀκούομεν. ἀγνοεῖ γὰρ ὁ Ἄργος, ὡς αὐτῶν ἐστιν τῆς χώρας.
If then the Achelous is among you; for we hear the name. For Argus does not know that it is in their country.
ἀναπιδύειν φησὶν οὖν τὸν Ἴστρον εἰς τὸν Ἀχελῶον διὰ τὸ τὰς πηγὰς αὐτῷ παρέχεσθαι. L
He says, then, that the Ister rises again into the Achelous because it supplies its sources. L
295. αἴσιον: fitting. Lᶢ P
296. ὁλκός: the course of the star. Lᶢ (P)

p.seg: ἐπέμενον γὰρ αἱ αὐταὶ τῶν ἀνέμων πνοαὶ καὶ ἡ φανεῖσα αὐτοῖς οὐρανία λαμπηδὼν ἡ τὸν ἐπὶ Ἴστρον διάπλουν σημαίνουσα.

div.p: 301-02. ἐπεὶ πνοιαί τε: for the same gusts of winds remained and the heavenly brightness that appeared to them, signifying the voyage through the Ister.
διαφωνοῦσι δὲ οἱ περὶ τοῦ ἔκπλου τῶν Ἀργοναυτῶν τοῦ ἐκ Κόλχων γεγραφότες. 〈. . .〉 ὡς καὶ Καλλίμαχος (fg 563 Schn.)· φησὶ δὲ Ἀπολλώνιος ὑποστρέψαι αὐτοὺς ἐναντίως Καλλιμάχῳ.
Those who have written about the voyage of the Argonauts from Colchis disagree. 〈...〉 as also Callimachus (fr. 563 Schn.); but Apollonius says that they returned contrary to Callimachus.

p.seg: τῶν Κόλχων οἱ μὲν διὰ τῶν Κυανέων πετρῶν ἔπλευσαν, ἄλλοι δὲ μετὰ Ἀψύρτου Ἴστρον ἔσχον. L

div.p: 303-06a. Κόλχοι δ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλοι: of the Colchians, some sailed through the Cyanean rocks, others with Apsyrtus made for the Ister. L

p.seg: τρία στόματα ἔχει ὁ Ἴστρος, ὧν ἓν λέγεται Καλὸν στόμα, ὥς φησι Τιμάγητος ἐν τῷ Περὶ λιμένων (fg 2 M. IV 519)· εἰς ὅ φησι πλεῦσαι τὸν Ἄψυρτον.

div.p: b. And fair through its mouth: the Ister has three mouths, of which one is called the Fair Mouth, as Timagetus says in his work On Harbours (fr. 2 M. IV 519); into this he says Apsyrtus sailed.

div.p: c. 〈mouth:〉 of the Ister. Gᶢ Sᵐ

p.seg: τὸ Ἰόνιον πέλαγος τῆς Ἰταλίας, εἰς ὃ ἐκδίδωσιν ὁ Ἀδρίας· διὸ καί τινες αὐτὸ Ἀδρίαν ὀνομάζουσιν.

div.p: 308a. uttermost of the Ionian sea: the Ionian sea is off Italy, into which the Adriatic discharges; therefore some call it the Adriatic.

p.seg: πρὸς τῇ Ἰταλίᾳ οὕτω καλούμενον. ὠνομάσθη δὲ ἀπὸ Ἰονίου τὸ γένος Ἰλλυριοῦ, ὥς φησιν Θεόπομπος ἐν κα΄ (115 fg 128 a J.)· τινὲς δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς γενομένης πλάνης τῇ Ἰοῖ.

div.p: b. The Ionian sea is so called near Italy. It was named after Ionius, an Illyrian by birth, as Theopompus says in his twenty-first book (115 fr. 128a J.); but some say from the wandering of Io.

p.seg: Ἐρατοσθένης ἐν γ΄ Γεωγραφικῶν (fg III B 98 Berger) νῆσον εἶναι ἐν τῷ Ἴστρῳ φησὶ τρίγωνον, ἴσην Ῥόδῳ, ἣν Πεύκην λέγεσθαι διὰ τὸ πολλὰς ἔχειν πεύκας.

div.p: 310. three-pronged: Eratosthenes in the third book of his Geography (fr. III B 98 Berger) says that there is a triangular island in the Ister, equal in size to Rhodes, which is called Peuce because it has many pine trees.

p.seg: περὶ τὸν περὶ τὴν Πεύκην ἀγκῶνα δύο εἶναί φησι στόματα τοῦ Ἴστρου, ὧν τὸ μὲν καλεῖται Νάρηκος, τὸ δὲ Καλὸν στόμα, ἐν ᾧ τάχιον οἱ Κόλχοι σὺν Ἀψύρτῳ ἔπλευσαν.

div.p: 311-14. And on both sides two: around the bend near Peuce he says there are two mouths of the Ister, of which one is called Narex, the other the Fair Mouth, by which the Colchians with Apsyrtus sailed more quickly.

p.seg: οἱ περὶ τὸν Ἰάσονα ἄνωθεν τῆς νήσου διὰ τοῦ Νάρηκος στόματος ἔπλευσαν. οἱ δὲ νομεῖς δόξαντες τὰς ναῦς — πάσας ἀκουαστέον — θαλάσσια θηρία εἶναι, δείσαντες εἰς φυγὴν ἐτράπησαν. L

div.p: 315-18a. But they high above the island: those with Jason sailed from above the island through the mouth of Narex. But the herdsmen, thinking that the ships—all of them, one must understand—were sea monsters, took fright and turned to flight. L

p.seg: οἱ κάθυγροι τόποι καὶ τεναγώδεις. δεῖ δὲ ἀκούειν ἑκατέρωθεν τοὺς νομεῖς πεφευγότας. L

div.p: b. Meadows are low-lying, marshy places. One must understand that the herdsmen fled on both sides. L

p.seg: τοῖς ἐπὶ τῆς Εὐρώπης Θρᾳξὶν ὅμοροί εἰσιν οἱ Σκύθαι.

div.p: 320a. Neither then with the Thracians: the Scythians are neighbours to the Thracians in Europe.

p.seg: ἔστι δὲ καὶ σίγυννος εἶδος δόρατος παρώνυμον τῷ ἔθνει.

div.p: b. 〈nor the Sigynni: . . .〉 There is also a sigynnus, a kind of spear, named after the tribe.

W 50 | lac. ind. W, ubi P praestat καὶ Σίγυνοι δὲ ἔθνος Σκυθικόν

p.seg: Λαύριον πεδίον τῆς Σκυθίας. τῆς δὲ Σκυθίας ἔθνη νε΄ Τιμῶναξ ἀναγράφει ἐν α΄ Περὶ Σκυθῶν (fg 1 M. IV 522). 〈. . .〉 κατὰ δὲ τὸ τῶν Σίνδων πεδίον σχίζεται ὁ ποταμὸς Ἴστρος, καὶ τὸ μὲν αὐτοῦ ῥεῦμα εἰς τὸν Ἀδρίαν, τὸ δὲ εἰς τὸν Εὔξεινον πόντον εἰσβάλλει. τὸ δὲ Σίνδοι Ἡρωδιανὸς ἐν τῷ ϛ΄ τῆς Καθόλου (I 142, 20 L.) βαρυτονεῖν φησι δεῖν· τινὲς δὲ ὀξυτονοῦσιν, οὐκ εὖ. καὶ Ἱππῶναξ (fg 68 A B. II 484) δὲ μνημονεύει, πρὸς τὸ ‘Σινδικὸν διάσφαγμα’. Ἑλλάνικος δὲ ἐν τῷ Περὶ ἐθνῶν φησι (4 fg 69 J.)· ‘Βόσπορον διαπλεύσαντι Σίνδοι, ἄνω δὲ τούτων Μαιῶται Σκύθαι’.

div.p: 321-22. Nor those around Laurium: Laurium is a plain of Scythia. Timonax in the first book of his work On Scythians (fr. 1 M. IV 522) records fifty-five tribes of Scythia. 〈. . .〉 At the plain of the Sindi the river Ister divides, and one stream of it flows into the Adriatic, the other into the Euxine Sea. Herodian in the sixth book of his General Prosody (I 142, 20 L.) says that the word Sindi should be barytone; but some make it oxytone, incorrectly. Hipponax (fr. 68 A B. II 484) also mentions it, with reference to the 'Sindic strait'. Hellanicus in his work On Peoples says (4 fr. 69 J.): 'After crossing the Bosporus one comes to the Sindi, and above them the Maeotian Scythians'.

p.seg: Ἄγγουρον ὄρος πλησίον Ἴστρου τοῦ ποταμοῦ. μνημονεύει δὲ αὐτοῦ Τιμάγητος ἐν Λιμέσιν (fg 5 M. IV 520). ὁ δὲ Καυλιακὸς σκόπελος τῆς Σκυθίας πλησίον τοῦ Ἴστρου, οὗ μνημονεύει Πολέμων ἐν Κτίσεσιν Ἰταλικῶν καὶ Σικελικῶν πόλεων (fg 38 M. III 126). γράφεται [Ἄγγουρον ὄρος] καὶ Ἄγτυρον ὄρος καὶ Ἀγγύρου ὄρεος, ἀντὶ δὲ τοῦ Καυλιακοῖο· Καυκαείοιο. φησὶ δὲ κατὰ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρος τὸν Ἴστρον διασχιζόμενον τὸ μὲν εἰς τὸν Ἀδρίαν, τὸ δὲ εἰς τὸν Εὔξεινον ῥεῖθρον εἰσβάλλειν.

div.p: 323-26a. Of the Angurum mountain: Angurum is a mountain near the river Ister. Timagetus mentions it in his work On Harbours (fr. 5 M. IV 520). The Cauliacan rock is in Scythia near the Ister, which Polemon mentions in his Foundations of Italian and Sicilian Cities (fr. 38 M. III 126). It is written [Angurum mountain] also as Agtyrum mountain and Angyri mountain, and instead of Cauliacan: Caucaean. He says that at this mountain the Ister divides and one stream flows into the Adriatic, the other into the Euxine.
b. 〈Caucaean:〉 it is written Cauliacan. Lᶢ

p.seg: τὸν Ἀδρίαν φησί· ἐνταῦθα γὰρ τὸν Κρόνον κατῳκηκέναι 〈φασίν〉.

div.p: 327. Cronian sea: he means the Adriatic; for there they say Cronus dwelt.
336. 〈to the shores:〉 it is written "to the seas." Lᵐ

p.seg: κατ’ ἐκεῖνον τὸν τόπον φησὶ τοὺς Ἀργοναύτας, τὸ πλῆθος τῶν Κόλχων φοβηθέντας, εἴκειν αὐτοῖς καὶ βούλεσθαι μὲν τὸ κῶας ἔχειν καὶ μὴ παρασχεῖν, τὴν δὲ Μήδειαν — ἦν γὰρ τὸ κατ’ αὐτὴν δίκαιον ἀμφήριστον — παραθέσθαι τῇ Ἀρτέμιδι ἐν τῷ αὐτῆς

div.p: 338-49a. 〈There:〉 In that place, he says, the Argonauts, fearing the multitude of the Colchians, yielded to them and wished to keep the fleece and not hand it over, but to entrust Medea—for the justice concerning her was disputed—to Artemis in her temple, until someone should judge whether she ought to be given back to her father or to the Argonauts. L

div.p: ἱερῷ, ἕως τις δικάσῃ, πότερον αὐτὴν ἀποδοτέον τῷ πατρὶ ἢ τοῖς Ἀργοναύταις. L
temple, until someone should judge whether she ought to be given back to her father or to the Argonauts. L
b. 〈by agreement:〉 by reconciliation. Gᶢ

p.seg: ὀνειδίζουσα τῷ Ἰάσονί φησι ξίφει αὐτὸν αὐτὴν διαχειρίσασθαι, ἵνα ἀξίαν ἀπολάβῃ χάριν τοῦ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔρωτος. ἐν ἤθει δὲ τοῦτο εἶπεν. L

div.p: 373-75. 〈Or you then:〉 Reproaching Jason, she says that he should kill her with a sword, so that she may receive a worthy return for her love for him. She said this in character. L
380. 〈wretchedly:〉 laboriously. Gᶢ

p.seg: ἀντὶ τοῦ καταπονούμενος καὶ στρεβλούμενος. Lᵐ P

div.p: 384. being distressed: instead of "being worn out and tortured." Lᵐ P

p.seg: τῇ σῇ κακοτροπίᾳ καὶ ἀβουλίᾳ, ὅτι ἐπιώρκησας. Lᵐ (P)

div.p: 387. by your fickleness: by your evil disposition and thoughtlessness, because you swore falsely. Lᵐ (P)
406. 〈Truly:〉 desirable things. Gᶢ Sᵐ

p.seg: ἐπὶ γὰρ τοῖς κακοῖς, φησί, κακὰ δεῖ βουλεύεσθαι. προῄρηται οὖν καὶ τὸν Ἄψυρτον ἀνελεῖν ἐπὶ τοῖς προγεγενημένοις ἁμαρτήμασιν ὑπ’ αὐτῆς. Lᵐ

div.p: 411-13. 〈with unseemly:〉 For in the face of evils, she says, one must plan evils. She has therefore chosen to kill Apsyrtus as well, on account of the sins previously committed by her. Lᵐ

p.seg: εἴ πως, φησί, πείσαιμι τὸν Ἄψυρτον μόνον πρὸς μόνην ἥκειν, φιλίαν πρὸς αὐτὸν συνθεμένη. Lᵐ

div.p: 417-18. 〈If somehow:〉 If somehow, she says, I could persuade Apsyrtus to come alone to me alone, having made a pact of friendship with him. Lᵐ

p.seg: ἐν τῇ Νάξῳ. Καλλίμαχος (fg 165 Schn.)· ‘ἐν Δίῃ· τὸ γὰρ ἔσκε παλαίτερον οὔνομα Νάξῳ.’ Lᵐ P

div.p: 425. Dia: on Naxos. Callimachus (fr. 165 Schn.): "in Dia; for that was the older name for Naxos." Lᵐ P
428-29a. with embroideries: with ornaments. Lᵐ (P)

p.seg: οὐδαμῶς ἂν τὸν πέπλον ἐκεῖνον ψηλαφῶν ἢ καθορῶν τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν πληρώσειας. Lᵐ

div.p: b. not touching it: in no way could you satisfy your desire by touching or beholding that robe. Lᵐ

p.seg: ἄκρως μεθύων ἀκράτῳ ἢ νέκταρι. Lᵐ (P)

div.p: 432. tipsy: extremely drunk with unmixed wine or nectar. Lᵐ (P)
433. daughter of Minos: Ariadne. Lᶢ (P)

p.seg: τὸν ἔρωτα εἶναι μέγα στύγημα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις λέγει. L

div.p: 445. 〈great abomination:〉 He says that love is a great abomination to humans. L

p.seg: μόνος δὲ πρὸς τὴν Μήδειαν μετιὼν ὁ Ἄψυρτος πεῖραν ἐλάμβανεν, ὡς ἔτι ὢν ἁπαλὸς καὶ δόλων ἄπειρος, εἰ βουληθείη προδοῦναι τοὺς Ἀργοναύτας, τὸν καθ’ αὑτοῦ δόλον οὐκ ἐπιστάμενος. L

div.p: 459-62. alone and face to face: Apsyrtus, going alone to Medea, was testing whether, being still tender and inexperienced in wiles, she might wish to betray the Argonauts, not knowing the plot against himself. L

p.seg: ἡ Μήδεια ἀπεστράφη τοῦ Ἀψύρτου ἀναιρουμένου, ἵνα μὴ τὸν φόνον αὐτοῦ ἴδῃ. L

div.p: 465-67. she turned her eyes away: Medea turned away from Apsyrtus as he was being killed, so as not to see his murder. L

p.seg: τὸν δὲ Ἄψυρτον ὁ Ἰάσων ἔπληξεν ὡς τις βοῦν καταβάλλων. L

div.p: 468. 〈And him, like an ox-slayer:〉 Jason struck Apsyrtus like someone felling an ox. L
470. Brygi: a people of Illyria.
471. 〈in the forecourt:〉 He used "forecourt" loosely for the pronaos.

p.seg: τῆς δὲ Μηδείας ὁ Ἄψυρτος ἀποθνῄσκων τὴν καλύπτραν καὶ τὸν πέπλον ἐρύθηνε τῷ ἑαυτοῦ αἵματι. L

div.p: 473-74. 〈her veil:〉 As Apsyrtus was dying, he stained Medea's veil and robe with his own blood. L

p.seg: οἱ δολοφονοῦντες ἀρχαίως ἀκρωτηριασματά τινα ἐποίουν τοῦ ἀναιρουμένου καὶ ταῦτα λαβόντες ἐξήρτων τοῦ τραχήλου αὐτοῦ. τῶν δὲ καλουμένων ἀκρωτηριασμάτων 〈. . .〉 ἄπειρα καὶ πολλὰ ἐξάργματα. ἔπειτα τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ λαβόντες, τρὶς εἰς τὸ στόμα ἀπέπτυον. τοῦτο δὲ ἐποίουν πρὸς τὸ ἐξιλάσασθαι τὴν δολοφονίαν.

div.p: 477-79. cut from the dead: Those who killed by treachery in ancient times would cut off certain extremities of the slain and, taking them, would hang them from his neck. Of the so-called extremities 〈...〉 countless and many appendages. Then, taking his blood, they spat it out three times into their mouths. They did this to expiate the treacherous murder.

div.note: 8 sch. II 90/93 cum loc. sim. | 13 Et. Gen. (AB) ἀπάργματα: Ἀπολλώνιος ὁ τὰ Ἀργοναυτικά, οἷον IV 475—479 (hucusque A, om. B). 〈ἐξάργματα καὶ add. Reitzenstein Ind. lect. Rost. 1890/91, 4〉 ἀπάργματα λέγεται τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν τραγῳδιῶν λεγόμενα μασχαλίσματα, ταῦτα δέ ἐστι τὰ τοῦ φονευθέντος ἀκρωτήρια (ταῦτα — άκρ. A, om. B). ἦν γάρ τι νόμιμον (A, νομικῆ B) τοῖς δολοφονήσασιν ἀφοσιῶσαι τὸν φόνον διὰ τοῦ δολοφονηθέντος ἀκρωτηριασμοῦ. τὰ δὲ ἀκρωτήρια εἴροντες καὶ συρράπτοντες διὰ τῶν τοῦ νεκροῦ μασχαλῶν καὶ τοῦ τραχήλου, περιετίθεσαν τῷ νεκρῷ, καθά φησι Σοφοκλῆς (El. 444 sq.)· ‘ὑφ’ ἧς θανὼν ἄτιμος ὥστε δυσμενὴς ἐμασχαλίσθη (B, -ην A)’. ὅτι δὲ καὶ ἐγεύοντο τοῦ αἵματος καὶ ἀπέπτυον, Αἰσχύλος (cf. fg 354 N.²) ἐν τοῖς †πρὸς λέβισιν† (ταῖς Περραιβίσιν Reitz.) ἱστορεῖ καὶ ἐν τῷ [περὶ del. idem] Λαΐῳ (ὅτι κτλ. A, om. B). Et. Gen. (AB) ἐξάργματα: εἰς τὸ ἀπάργματα. Et. Gen. (AB) ἐμασχαλίσθη (ἐκ τοῦ ῥητορικοῦ καὶ ἐξ ἄλλων) sch. Soph. El. 445 Hesych. Phot. Suid. μασχαλίσματα Suid. ἐμασχαλίσθη Plut. div.p: εἰς τὸ στόμα ἀπέπτυον. τοῦτο δὲ ἐποίουν πρὸς τὸ ἐξιλάσασθαι τὴν δολοφονίαν.
they spat it out into their mouths. They did this to expiate the treacherous murder.
481. Apsyrtians: a people named after Apsyrtus.

p.seg: μετὰ τὸν Ἀψύρτου θάνατον πλεῖν ἐπὶ τοὺς λοιποὺς Κόλχους, λέγων ὅτι ὄρθρου ἰδόντες τὸ πεπραγμένον 〈οὐχ〉 ἑνὶ λόγῳ χρώμενοι διώξουσιν ἡμᾶς. L

div.p: 495-99. Peleus advises that after the death of Apsyrtus they sail against the remaining Colchians, saying that at dawn, having seen what was done, they will pursue us, not with one accord.
500. <kedoontai:> they are scattered.

p.seg: αὕτη ἡ Ἠλεκτρὶς ἐγγύς ἐστι τοῦ Ἠριδανοῦ ποταμοῦ.

div.p: 505. <Electrida:> this Electris is near the river Eridanus.

p.seg: τῆς Ἀργοῦς οὐκ ἐπανῆλθον φοβούμενοι τὸν Αἰήτην, ἀλλ’ οἱ μὲν αὐτῶν ᾤκησαν ὅπου ὁ Ἄψυρτος ἐδολοφονήθη, μετὰ τῶν κληθέντων ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ Ἀψυρτέων, οἱ δὲ ἐν Ἰλλυρίᾳ, ὅπου οἱ Ἐγχελεῖς περὶ τὰ Κεραύνια ὄρη. Lᵐ (P)

div.p: 507-21. The Colchians, when the Argo set sail, did not return for fear of Aeetes, but some of them settled where Apsyrtus was treacherously slain, with the people called Apsyrtians after him, and others in Illyria, where the Encheleis are around the Ceraunian mountains.

p.seg: ἔθνος περὶ τὴν Ἰλλυρίαν, ἀπὸ Ὕλλου τοῦ Ἡρακλέους καὶ Μελίτης ὠνομασμένον.

div.p: 524. Hylleans: a people around Illyria, named from Hyllus, son of Heracles and Melite.

p.seg: πεῦσιν, χρησμὸν αἰτησόμενος παρὰ τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος.

div.p: 531. hierēn peusome<nos>: inquiry, about to ask an oracle from Apollo.
532-33. hopēi chthonos hidryth<eien>: the Hylleans, having received

A). | 14 Et. Gen. (B) Ὑλλήων : IV 521. 524 ἔστι δὲ ἔθνος Κελτικῆς Ὑλλεῖς, ἀπὸ Ὕλλου βασιλέως αὐτῶν, υἱοῦ (Et. M., ὡς οὐ B) Μελίτης καὶ Ἡρακλέους. sch. 1149/50 Steph. Byz. Ὑλλεῖς: ἔθνος Ἰλλυρικόν, ἀπὸ Ὕλλου τοῦ Ἡρακλέους καὶ Μελίτης τῆς Αἰγαίου τοῦ ποταμοῦ, ὡς Ἀπολλώνιος τετάρτῳ Ἀργοναυτικῶν. Eust. Dion. Per. 384 cf. W 63

div.p: παρὰ Ἰάσονος τρίποδα μισθὸν τῆς μηνύσεως τῆς ὁδοῦ, ἔκρυψαν ὑπὸ γῆν, ἐπεὶ ὁ χρησμὸς ἐκέλευσεν, ἔνθα ἂν ὁ τρίπους ᾖ, ἀπόρθητον εἶναι τὴν πόλιν. LᴳM Sᴹ P
a tripod from Jason as a reward for showing the way, hid it under the ground, since the oracle commanded that wherever the tripod should be, the city would be unravaged.
534. hode: the tripod, clearly.

p.seg: Μάκρις τὸ παλαιὸν ἐλέγετο ἡ Σχερία, ὠνομασμένη ἀπὸ τῆς Διονύσου τροφοῦ. ἔνθα φησὶ τὸν Ἡρακλέα παραγενόμενον, τὸν τῶν παίδων αὑτοῦ φόνον καθαρθησόμενον, Μελίτην τὴν Αἰγαίου τοῦ ποταμοῦ θυγατέρα γεγαμηκέναι, ἐξ ἧς ἔσχε τὸν Ὕλλον· ὃς ἀκμάσας οὐκ ἠθέλησε τῷ Ναυσιθόῳ ὑποταγῆναι, ἀλλὰ τοὺς Φαίακας συνήγαγεν εἰς τὴν Κρονίαν θάλασσαν καὶ κατῴκισεν.

div.p: 540-49a. Makrin t' eisaphika<ne>: Macris was the ancient name of Scheria, named after the nurse of Dionysus. There, they say, Heracles came to be purified of the murder of his children, and married Melite, daughter of the river Aegaeus, from whom he had Hyllus; who, when he grew up, did not wish to be subject to Nausithous, but gathered the Phaeacians to the Cronian sea and settled them.
b. hyp' ophrysi: with knitted brows.

p.seg: πυνθάνεται τῆς Μούσης ὁ ποιητής, ποῦ τὸν πλοῦν ἐποίησαν οἱ Ἀργοναῦται μετὰ τὸν Ἀψύρτου θάνατον καὶ πῶς εἰς θάλασσαν ἦλθον.

div.p: 552-56a. alla, theai, pōs: the poet asks the Muse where the Argonauts sailed after the death of Apsyrtus and how they came to the sea.

μέμφονται δέ τινες τὸν Ἀπολλώνιον ὡς περὶ τούτους τοὺς χρόνους εἰρηκότα τὴν Ἰταλίαν Αὐσονίαν· ὑστέροις γὰρ χρόνοις τῶν Ἀργοναυτῶν οὕτω κέκληται ἀπὸ Αὔσονος τοῦ Ὀδυσσέως καὶ Καλυψοῦς. ἐροῦμεν δέ, ὅτι ἐπεὶ αὐτὸς ὁ ποιητὴς οὕτως ὠνόμαζεν, εἰ καὶ μὴ κατὰ τοὺς ἐκείνων χρόνους ἦν.

Some criticize Apollonius for having said that Italy was called Ausonia at that time; for it was called so in later times than the Argonauts, from Auson, son of Odysseus and Calypso. But we shall say that since the poet himself named it so, even if it was not according to the times of those men.

p.seg: περὶ τὴν Ἰταλίαν εἰσὶ τρεῖς Λιγυστιάδες καλούμεναι, διότι οἰκοῦνται ὑπὸ τῶν Λιγύων· Στοιχάδες δὲ διὰ τὸ στοίχῳ τετάχθαι.

div.p: b. nēsous te Ligystidas: near Italy there are three islands called Ligystiades, because they are inhabited by the Ligurians; and Stoechades because they are arranged in a row.

p.seg: μετὰ τὴν πεῦσιν ἐμπνευσθεὶς ἐντεῦθεν ἄρχεται τοῦ διηγήματος. Lᵐ (P)

div.p: 557. auton pou: after the inquiry, inspired, he begins the narrative from here.

p.seg: Λίβυρνοι ἔθνος οἰκοῦντες ταύτας τὰς νήσους, Ἴσσαν τε καὶ Δυσκέλαδον καὶ Πιτύειαν· μεθ’ ἃς εἰς Κέρκυραν ἦλθον. τὴν δὲ Πιτυοῦσσαν καλουμένην Πιτύειαν εἶπεν Ὁμήρῳ (Β 829) ἑπόμενος.

div.p: 564-66. hexeiēs plēthonto: the Liburnians, a people inhabiting these islands, Issa and Dysceladus and Pityeia; after which they came to Corcyra. He called the island called Pityussa Pityeia, following Homer (B 829).
